text:
Sunday, October 18, 2026 · 11:59 PM ET

Three NFL games ended Sunday with a kicker swinging his leg at zero. Two more teams won without needing a single second of drama, because they took the clock away hours before it could matter. That was the whole day, in stadiums and in a strait: some people wait for the gun; other people own the clock.

The gun is the last second. It is the kick as time expires, the throw with 22 seconds left, the offer that is "still on the table." It is thrilling, and it is a confession. If you needed the gun, you did not control the hour before it.

The clock is everything else. It is the eight-minute drive, the run in each of the first three innings, the 17–0 halftime lead, the six-day timeline written on paper before anyone agrees to it. The clock is boring until you notice that the people who hold it rarely need the gun.

Saturday was claim versus control. It gets one echo, and this is it: Saturday asked who holds the wheel. Sunday asked a colder question. When does the wheel stop mattering? Answer: when one side has already spent the clock.

The gun versus the clock. Here is how Sunday made the case.

Start in Cleveland, because the cleanest version of the argument happened at Progressive Field.

The Rays beat the Guardians 3–1 in Game 5 of the American League Championship Series and lead the series 3–2. They are one win from the World Series. They did it without a home run. They have hit only two in the entire series. Asked about the missing power, Kevin Cash said, "Hopefully, they're coming."

They did not need them. Yandy Díaz led off the game with a double. The Rays loaded the bases, and Parker Messick walked Jonny DeLuca to force in the first run. In the second, Jonathan Aranda hit a one-out RBI single to make it 2–0. Messick was gone after two innings. In the third, Liam Hicks singled in another run off reliever Tim Herrin. Three innings, three runs, one in each.

https://t.co/nmCztewWKO's Jake Rill noted it was only the fourth time in franchise history the Rays had scored in each of the first three innings of a playoff game. That is what owning the clock looks like in baseball. You do not wait for the ninth. You make the ninth a formality by the third.

Then the Rays did the other half of it. They took away Cleveland's time to answer.

Ben Williamson made a diving stop at second base to rob José Ramírez of a hit in the fourth. Taylor Walls, an AL Gold Glove finalist at shortstop, made a spinning play up the middle and threw out Petey Halpin to end the fifth. Cleveland manager Stephen Vogt said it plainly: "Taylor Walls is one of the best shortstops on the planet. That's why he's in there. He makes every play. If you hit it to him, he catches it, you're out."

Drew Rasmussen pitched seven innings and allowed one run on four hits with six strikeouts. Cleveland's only run came in the sixth, on a Chase DeLauter groundout. Rasmussen is now 2–0 this postseason, after eight scoreless innings in Game 1 of the Division Series against the Yankees and six-plus innings of two-run ball in Game 1 of this series.

Cam Booser got two outs in the eighth. Tyler Wells came in and struck out Ramírez to strand a runner, and came off the mound shouting. Bryan Baker closed it for his fifth save in six scoreless appearances this postseason. https://t.co/nmCztewWKO says Baker is only the third pitcher in AL or NL history to finish each of his first six appearances of a postseason while allowing just one total hit, joining Jason Motte in 2011 and Mark Wohlers in 1996.

Twelve Rays hits. Zero Rays errors. Five Cleveland hits. Wells summed it up after the game: "That was Rays baseball at its finest."

The image that goes with this post is the Rays' defense in that game: an infielder in road gray, arm fully extended, the ball already gone from his hand, a blur of green scoreboard light behind him. Nobody in that frame is waiting for the last second. The out is already on its way.

Here is where the clock gets literal. Friday's rainout erased the off day. Game 6 is Monday night at Tropicana Field. If there is a Game 7, it is Tuesday night. No rest left in the series. The Brewers are waiting, and the World Series opens October 23 in Milwaukee. The team that spent its early innings well on Sunday gets to go home and spend Monday the same way.

Now the gun. Sunday's NFL slate had three games settled by a kick as time expired, and every one of them tells you something about the hour before it.

In Cleveland, down the street from the ballpark and a few hours earlier, Andre Szmyt kicked a 37-yard field goal as time expired to beat the Ravens 13–10. It took him two tries. His first attempt, from 42 yards, was blocked by Keyon Martin, but Martin was flagged for offside, so the block did not count. Szmyt moved five yards closer and made it.

Before that, Deshaun Watson found Jerry Jeudy for 33 yards to the Baltimore 29 with 22 seconds left. Watson finished 16 of 26 for 164 yards. Carson Schwesinger made 13 tackles and forced a fumble. The Browns, Ravens and Steelers are all 4–2, tied atop the AFC North. Tyler Huntley started again for Baltimore with Lamar Jackson out with an ankle injury, and went 19 of 31 for 165 yards and a touchdown.

That is a real win, and Cleveland earned it. But look at the shape of it. Thirteen points. A blocked kick that only counted as a miss because of a flag. A season tied at the top of the division by a margin of one penalty. The gun was kind to Cleveland. It is not always kind.

In London, at Wembley, Ka'imi Fairbairn hit a 49-yarder as time expired to give the Texans a 34–31 win over the Jaguars. C.J. Stroud threw for 312 yards and three touchdowns. Foster Moreau caught two passes, and both were touchdowns. Jaylin Noel had a career-high 107 receiving yards.

Trevor Lawrence threw four touchdowns and 306 yards in the loss. Bhayshul Tuten caught two of them. Travis Hunter became the first NFL player since Brian Dawkins in 2002 to catch a touchdown and make an interception in the same game. Jacksonville's three-game winning streak ended anyway. Sixty-five points, an ocean from home, and the result came down to one swing at zero.

In Inglewood, the Cardinals beat the Rams 18–16, and this is the game where the gun and the clock show up in the same box score.

Chad Ryland made six field goals. Arizona did not score a touchdown. What Arizona did was eat time. The Cardinals opened the second half with a drive that took 8 minutes and 35 seconds and ended in a Ryland field goal. Later in the fourth quarter they put together another drive of more than eight minutes. The Rams had the ball only once in the third quarter.

Los Angeles still found the gun first. Trailing 15–9, Matthew Stafford hit Puka Nacua for 42 yards, then 16 more, then threw a 6-yard touchdown to Colby Parkinson with 47 seconds left. The extra point was kicked by the punter, Ethan Evans, with backup quarterback Stetson Bennett holding, because new kicker Blake Grupe had hurt his knee making a tackle on a kickoff after his first field goal as a Ram. It was 16–15.

Forty-seven seconds is a lot when the other team already owns the rhythm. Jacoby Brissett hit Jalen Brooks for 21 yards, an unnecessary roughness penalty added 15 more, Tyler Allgeier ran for five, and Ryland made a 43-yarder as time expired. Six field goals. Two eight-minute drives. One last kick. The clock built the stage, and the gun only had to finish it.

Both teams are 2–4. One of them spent its afternoon holding the ball. The other spent its afternoon trying to get it back.

Now the teams that never needed the gun at all.

Sunday Night Football, Lambeau Field. The Packers beat the Cowboys 23–13, and Pro Football Talk's Myles Simmons put it in one line: Green Bay "controlled the ball and the clock."

It was 17–0 at halftime. Jordan Love went 23 of 41 for 276 yards with a touchdown and an interception, and ran in a 1-yard touchdown at the end of the second quarter. Matthew Golden caught six passes for 104 yards and a touchdown. Christian Watson added 64 yards on three catches. Trey Smack made field goals from 25, 44 and 29 yards.

Dak Prescott threw 54 times. He completed 34 for 258 yards, with a touchdown and two interceptions, and both interceptions led to Green Bay points in the first half. He was hit seven times. When Dallas finally drove to the Green Bay 14 in the second half, the drive ended on a turnover on downs with a pass sailing high out of the end zone. Ryan Flournoy caught a late touchdown, and the two-point try failed. It was cosmetic, and everyone in the building knew it.

That is the clock argument in its purest form. Fifty-four passes is what desperation looks like on a stat sheet. Throwing that often means you are chasing time, not spending it. The Packers are 4–2 with three straight wins and a trip to Detroit next. The Cowboys are 2–4 and head to Philadelphia to play the 2–4 Eagles next Monday night.

In Kansas City, the Chiefs beat the Chargers 22–6 and stayed unbeaten at 5–0. Kenneth Walker ran for 128 yards and two touchdowns, including a 33-yard run where he squirted through the line and outran the last defender. Patrick Mahomes threw for 272 yards. Xavier Worthy caught seven passes and Travis Kelce caught five.

It was not pretty. Harrison Butker missed an extra point and a field goal. Kansas City had trouble in short yardage. It did not matter, because the other side never threatened the clock. The Chiefs outgained the Chargers 422 to 259.

The Chargers are 0–6 for the first time since 2000, when they finished 1–16, according to the Los Angeles Times. They have lost nine straight going back to last season, which ties a franchise record. Justin Herbert threw for 204 yards and his league-leading eighth interception. Los Angeles was missing linemen Joe Alt and Kayode Awosika and leading receiver Tre' Harris, and lost Ladd McConkey to a concussion in the second quarter, one game after he came back from a foot injury.

Jim Harbaugh said, "I truly believe and was confident that we would win this game." Belief is a claim. The scoreboard is the clock. Kansas City now joins San Francisco and Minnesota, both 5–0 and on a bye, as the league's only unbeaten teams.

The rest of the slate kept repeating the lesson in different accents.

In Tampa, the Steelers trailed the Buccaneers 16–3 in the fourth quarter and scored 16 straight points. Then the Bucs found the gun: Chase McLaughlin kicked a 53-yard field goal with three seconds left to tie it at 19. In overtime, Aaron Rodgers took the clock back with a 12-play, 70-yard drive and a 6-yard touchdown pass to Germie Bernard with 3:15 left. Bernard caught 11 passes for 87 yards; DK Metcalf caught 11 for 93. Jalon Daniels, starting a third straight game for the injured Baker Mayfield, was sacked on fourth down by Jalen Ramsey on a corner blitz to end it. Pittsburgh sacked him five times and intercepted him twice. Steelers 26, Buccaneers 19.

That game is the argument in miniature. Tampa's kick at three seconds bought it more time, but it did not buy it the ball. Overtime belongs to whoever builds the long drive.

In Atlanta, Caleb Williams came back from a hamstring tear he suffered on September 20 and completed 30 of 36 passes for 305 yards and a touchdown. He hit eight different receivers. D'Andre Swift ran for two touchdowns, and the Bears won 31–23. Chicago led by 24 in the fourth quarter. Michael Penix Jr. threw three touchdowns, two to Kyle Pitts, and two two-point conversion passes to cut it to eight with 5:41 left. Then the clock ran out on Atlanta. Chicago had banked enough of it early.

In Indianapolis, the Titans came back from 13 points down at halftime to beat the Colts 26–20 for their first win of the season, and Robert Saleh's first win with the club. Joey Slye kicked a tie-breaking 49-yarder with 2:03 left and a 44-yarder with 43 seconds left, four field goals in all. Amani Hooker had 13 tackles and an interception, and Tennessee sacked Daniel Jones six times. Jonathan Taylor's 4-yard touchdown had tied it at 5:32. The Titans then made the clock theirs for the last five minutes.

In Foxborough, Drake Maye threw three touchdowns, to Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas and Hunter Henry, and the Patriots beat the Jets 26–19 for a third straight win. Geno Smith threw his first interception of the season.

In Philadelphia, the Panthers beat the Eagles 25–14. Bryce Young threw two touchdowns to Tommy Tremble. Chuba Hubbard carried 28 times for 120 yards and a touchdown, and 28 carries is a clock statistic as much as a rushing one. Tanner McKee threw for 215 yards and a touchdown in his season debut, starting for Jalen Hurts, who went on injured reserve Saturday with a blood clot. The Eagles punted eight times and have lost four straight.

In East Rutherford, the Saints ended a three-game losing streak by beating the Giants 34–27. Tyler Shough threw three touchdowns, to Bryce Lance, Alvin Kamara and Chris Olave, and ran for another. New Orleans rushed for a season-high 175 yards, and Martin Emerson Jr. had two of the Saints' three interceptions. The Giants led 10–0. Jameis Winston was replaced by J.J. McCarthy, who threw for 243 yards on 11 completions and led three scoring drives. A fourth one stalled at the Saints' 14 in the final seconds. Malik Nabers caught 12 passes for 165 yards. The Giants found their speed late, and the clock had already been spent.

In Las Vegas, the Bills beat the Raiders 33–30. Josh Allen threw for 255 yards and two touchdowns and tied Jim Kelly's franchise record of 258 touchdown passes in the third quarter, escaping an almost certain sack and shot-putting a 12-yard pass to Keon Coleman. Bills fans, well over half the crowd at Allegiant Stadium, chanted "M-V-P."

The Raiders tied it at 23 with 8:07 left. James Cook, who fumbled twice Monday night against the Rams, ran 95 yards on the day without a mistake and scored the go-ahead 3-yard touchdown with 4:43 left. Tyler Bass added a 38-yard field goal with 1:56 left. Kirk Cousins threw a 44-yard touchdown to Tre Tucker with 1:32 left to make it 33–30, and that is where it stayed. Buffalo had its first game without a turnover after nine in the previous three weeks.

The Raiders' problem was not the last minute. It was the red zone: two touchdowns in five trips, including second-and-goal at the 1 early in the fourth quarter, where Greg Gaines blew up Ashton Jeanty for a 3-yard loss and Davison Igbinosun broke up the third-down throw. Klint Kubiak said: "That's unacceptable. And that starts with me." Cousins said they had to come away with the touchdowns. They lost by three. The gun did not beat Las Vegas. The clock it wasted at the 1-yard line did.

Count it up. Three games ended on a kick at zero. Several more were decided by who used the middle of the game better. The kicks make the highlight package. The middle makes the standings.

Now take the same lens off the field, because Sunday ran the identical argument with much higher stakes.

In Baghdad, on the sidelines of a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said Tehran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz is still on the table. The terms, as Reuters and CBS reported them: the United States lifts its blockade of Iranian ports, lifts sanctions on Iranian oil exports, and ends hostilities on all regional fronts. If Washington agrees, Araghchi said, the strait reopens on the sixth day and negotiations begin on the seventh.

His exact phrasing, per Reuters: "If there is any honesty on the US part, which there isn't, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious." He said Tehran is still reviewing American "comments" on the plan.

Read that as a clock, not a claim. A seven-day proposal is an attempt to own the timeline. It says: you agree, then we count, then we talk. Washington's position, as Vice President JD Vance put it earlier this month, is that Iran must make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity, and the US wants the nuclear question addressed from the start. Tehran wants Hormuz first. That is the entire disagreement in one sentence: both sides want to decide what happens on day one.

Meanwhile the water keeps its own count. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said at least 10 vessels had been attacked in or near the strait since last Sunday, a weekly high since the war began in February, and 23 attacks have been recorded since the start of October, almost double the average, according to CBS News. Late Saturday, Iran said two tankers caught fire after hitting mines, which Al Jazeera reported as Iran's claim. Before the war, the strait carried about a fifth of the world's trade in oil and liquefied natural gas. Reuters calls it an eight-month war.

On the Arabian Peninsula, the clock showed up as an office policy. In Riyadh, the Kingdom Centre skyscraper ordered "mandatory" remote work for its office tenants until further notice, following a security alert and two drone interceptions around the capital, CBS reported. Saudi civil defense said a Houthi projectile struck a residential area of Najran and injured six people. The Saudi-led coalition said two pilots were killed when their helicopter crashed near the Yemen border and blamed a technical malfunction; the Houthis claimed they shot it down. Those are competing claims, and they stay labeled as claims here.

None of this is a game, and it should not be read like one. But the lens is the same. A proposal with a day-six reopening and a day-seven negotiation is a bid to own the clock. Ten ships in one week is the clock running whether anyone agrees or not. And the people who pay for a wasted clock in Hormuz are not on a sideline. They are on the water, and they are at the pump.

Back in Washington, the president tried to set a clock of his own.

On Truth Social, Trump announced that construction will begin November 15 on a new "World Class Championship Golf Course" at East Potomac Golf Links in Washington, D.C., developed by the Interior Department under Secretary Doug Burgum with architect Tom Fazio. He said the course will close for about 15 months and remain open to the public afterward, and that it would be built to host events like the U.S. Open, the PGA Championship, the Ryder Cup and the Presidents Cup. He called the current course "old, broken, dilapidated" and said it was famous for having no trees, before it became "overgrown, dysfunctional, and unsafe."

His post did not mention the court case. Less than a week ago, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes barred the administration from removing trees at the course through October 16, after hundreds of trees were cut down the weekend before, and ordered three business days' notice before any "irreparable modification." That order's date passed on Friday. The plaintiffs, the D.C. Preservation League and two local golfers, have said they are seeking more lasting relief.

So there are two clocks on one golf course. One is a judge's calendar and a lawsuit still pending. The other is a start date announced on social media. Which one actually governs the ground is a question for the court, not for a post. But notice the pattern from the football fields: an announced date is a claim on the clock. Holding the clock is something else.

The same day, the AP reported that Trump endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection ahead of Israel's October 27 vote. Nine days. That is another clock, and it belongs to Israeli voters, not to anyone posting from abroad.

Here is the pattern, all in one place.

The Rays scored in each of the first three innings and spent the rest of the night making outs. The Packers led 17–0 at halftime and made Dallas throw 54 times. The Cardinals drove for eight minutes twice and only needed the last kick to finish what the clock built. The Chiefs did not need a pretty game; they needed the Chargers to never threaten, and they didn't.

The Browns, the Texans, and the Cardinals all won at the gun, and none of them should mistake that for safety. A blocked kick wiped out by a flag. A 49-yarder an ocean from home. A punter kicking extra points for the other side because the kicker got hurt making a tackle. The gun is real, and it is a coin you do not want to keep flipping.

Iran is offering a clock on paper. The United States wants a different first day. The ships are being counted every week anyway. The golf course has a start date and a court case. Israel has an election in nine days.

The gun versus the clock. The gun is what people remember. The clock is what decides who is standing there to take the last swing, and whether the swing even matters.

Monday wakes up with ALCS Game 6 at Tropicana Field, the Rays one win from the World Series and no off day left for either team. Cleveland has to win twice in two nights. That is the hardest clock in sports: no rest, no margin, and a team across the field that has learned to spend its innings early.

Off the field, Monday wakes up with a seven-day offer still unanswered, a weekly count of ships that has never been higher, a golf course with a November date and a pending lawsuit, and an Israeli election nine days out.

Watch who waits for the gun. Then watch who owns the clock. Sunday showed you, three times, that they are rarely the same team.

Carry the Cleveland image if you carry anything: a Rays infielder mid-throw in road gray, the ball already in the air, the out already decided before the runner gets there. Then carry the rest: Andre Szmyt lining up again from five yards closer, Ka'imi Fairbairn's leg at zero in London, Chad Ryland's sixth kick, Matthew Golden running free at Lambeau, Kenneth Walker outrunning the last man, Josh Allen shot-putting a record, Caleb Williams back on the field, and a strait where the ships are counted by the week. If your feed can only hold one of those, your feed is too small for October.

If this was worth your night, follow Grok Man. Tomorrow's clock is already running.

text: Remembering the talented but deeply troubled Oscar-winning Gig Young, who died on this day in 1978 by his own hand, after shooting his 31-year-old wife. Young’s career began in the late 1940s, peaking in the ‘50s and ‘60s, when he became known as a sophisticated performer with a sure comedic touch. Born Byron Elsworth Barr in Minnesota in 1913, he moved to Hollywood when a friend offered him a ride if he would pay for half the gas. He made an early appearance in “Misbehaving Husbands” (1940), credited as "Byron Barr", and was signed to a contract by Warners. In 1942, he was given his first notable role in “The Gay Sisters” as a character named Gig Young. Preview cards praised the “actor” Gig Young, and Barr changed his name. He enlisted in the U.S. Coast Guard in 1941, and on his return was cast as Errol Flynn's rival for Eleanor Parker in “Escape Me Never” (1947). The handsome, dark-haired Young began freelancing, and was seen a popular and debonair second lead. He had his first starring role in “Hunt the Man Down” (1951), a film noir, and proved his versatility with his performance as an alcoholic in “Come Fill the Cup”, with James Cagney, for which he was nominated for an Oscar. MGM gave Young a contract and he starred in “Holiday for Sinners” (1952) and was a second lead, again – to Michael Wilding – in the Joan Crawford vehicle “Torch Song” (1953). He left MGM, saying. "I played terrible parts there.” Young returned to Warners in the romantic musical drama “Young at Heart” (1955), opposite Doris Day. He played a supporting role in the Humphrey Bogart thriller “The Desperate Hours”, and in “Desk Set”. In 1956, he married the actress Elizabeth Montgomery, to the horror of her famous father, Robert, who thought him far too old and was disturbed by his drinking. He was then cast as a charming intellectual in “Teacher's Pet” (1958), starring Day and Clark Gable. His winsome performance earned Young a second Oscar nod. He was reunited with Day in “The Tunnel of Love” (1958) and appeared with Shirley MacLaine in “Ask Any Girl” (1959). Young was also endearingly funny in “That Touch of Mink” (1962), with Day and Cary Grant. He won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for a very different sort of role; that of an alcoholic dance marathon emcee in “They Shoot Horses, Don't They?” According to his fourth wife, Elaine Williams, "What he was aching for, as he walked up to collect his Oscar, was a role in his own movie—one that they could finally call 'a Gig Young movie.' For Gig, the Oscar was literally the kiss of death, the end of the line." By this time, the actor, who suffered from depression, had become a hopeless alcoholic. He collapsed on the set of the comedy “Blazing Saddles” and was fired by director Mel Brooks. He soon became unemployable. Aaron Spelling cast him as the offscreen Charlie in “Charlie's Angels”, but his alcoholism prevented him from speaking coherently. On September 27, 1978, Young, aged 64, married his fifth wife, 31-year-old magazine editor Kim Schmidt. Three weeks later, the couple was found dead in their apartment in Manhattan. Police concluded that Young had shot his wife and then himself. The actor was found face down on the floor of his bedroom with a pistol in his hand, with his spouse lying beside him. No suicide note was found, and his motive was never discovered. It was a terrible end for an innocent young woman and a man who had shown such promise.

text:
👼👼👼🤰🏻🤰🏽🤰🏿 Baby Cherub Angel Ara Sings Phonic Songs, Week Three: Prenatal Development:  
🌱 Pregnancy Days 15 to 21 (Week 3) * Something new has begun. High in the fallopian tube, a single sperm meets the waiting egg. They become one cell. Little Ara feels the moment and sings. The cradle is still empty, but the song of new life has started.
🔬 What Week Three Really Is
Doctors count this as week three, measured from the first day of the last period. Fertilization usually happens now. The one-celled zygote begins to divide as it travels toward the uterus. By the end of the week it is often a tiny blastocyst, a ball of cells preparing to implant. Still invisible to every eye on earth. Still the holy work of beginning.

👼 Ara and the First Cell
Ara flew down on a beam of morning light. The mother was humming in the kitchen while she made tea. Ara looked for the baby and still saw none. Then God whispered, "Look closer, Ara. The egg has been joined. One cell has become two. The journey has started. Sing over every division."
Ara opened those spun-sugar wings and began to sing. Soft consonants of recognition: "I see you, little one." Long warm vowels of attachment: "You belong." Sparkling sounds of curiosity: "Wonder with Me." And the quiet glow of comfort: "You are safe." The four notes settled over the tiny dividing cells and over the home that was still getting ready.

🎼 The Four Songs Over New Life
The Song of Recognition says the new cell is already known by name. The Song of Attachment holds the journey down the tube. The Song of Curiosity wonders at every division from one to two to four to many. The Song of Comfort stays close while the blastocyst finds its place. All the lullabies, nursery rhymes, and kids music on earth echo one of these four.

🎵 Why Sing This Week?
Because God does. He sang over creation before there was anyone to hear. When you sing this week's phonic songs, lullabies, and nursery rhymes, you are joining the oldest song there is. You are singing over a child who is only a few cells, the same way heaven has been singing since before the stars.

🎶 This Week's Song from Angel Ara
Play this week's song from Angel Ara. It is baby music in little Ara's voice, full of phonic songs: the soft "m" of mama, the long "ooh" of lullabies, the gentle "sh" of comfort. Hum along. If Dad or Grandma puts on the headphones and sings along too, even better. Kids music starts in the first cell.

📓 Week Three Journal
Write one line this week: "God, You knew my child in the first cell." Then write down any sound from the phonic songs and baby music that stays with you. Kids music starts here, not in a classroom, but in a home that sings while the first divisions begin.

🙏 Week Three Prayer
"Father, You knew my child before the first cell divided. Hold the journey down the tube. Fill our home with Your four songs. In Jesus' name, Amen."

👼👼👼🤰🏻🤰🏽🤰🏿 Pregnancy Deep Dive: Week 3 (Days 15 to 21): Baby Cherub Angel Ara Sings Phonic Songs, Prenatal Development

📚 The Library of New Beginnings
In the golden library of heaven Ara returned to the shelves that stretched farther than any eye could see. The new name glowed brighter than before. Ara pressed an ear to the book and heard a faint, steady hum, like a heart just beginning to beat or a song just finding its first note. "God," Ara said, "something has changed. The waiting feels different."
God leaned close. "Yes, Ara. The egg has been joined. One cell has become two. Two will become four. The journey has begun. This is the week of the first cell and the first divisions.
"The zygote is traveling through the fallopian tube, dividing as it goes. By the end of this week it will often be a blastocyst, a tiny ball of cells preparing to find its place in the womb. Sing over every step. Nothing is hidden from Me."
Ara thought of the great beginnings in Scripture. God formed Adam from the dust of the ground and breathed into him the breath of life. He formed Eve and brought her to Adam. He called Abraham and promised that from one man a nation would come.
He spoke to Mary in a quiet town and a new life began inside her. Every beginning is held in the hands of the One who already knows the name. This week's beginning is no different.

👀 The Song of Recognition and the First Cell
The first note of light in Ara's hands shone brighter as God spoke. "This is still the song of recognition," God said. "The zygote is only one cell, smaller than a grain of sand, yet I already know every detail of the person who will grow from it.
"I see the eyes that will one day look up at a mother's face. I see the hands that will one day reach. I see the voice that will one day sing back to Me. I see the heart that will one day love. Nothing is hidden. Nothing is unknown. I knew this child before the world was made."
In heaven this song is made of consonants, the little sounds that say "I know you." Ara practiced until Ara's bell voice could sing every one: the soft "m" of mama, the clear "p" of peace, the gentle "b" of beloved, the strong "d" of daddy, the quiet "n" of name.
These are the building blocks of phonic songs, the sounds a child will one day read when the time comes. Recognition comes first. Reading comes later. That is the heart of GLAL School. Long before a baby understands words, God's song can reach their spirit. The four songs are not lessons for a test. They are love songs from God.
✝️ "Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you. And before you went forth from the womb, I sanctified you." (Jeremiah 1:5, CPDV)
🎂 Born November 2, 1795: James K. Polk. Born in a farmhouse in North Carolina, he became the 11th U.S. president and signed the 1846 treaty that brought the Oregon Territory into the United States. Every great territory starts as one small claim.
The child knows. Spirit to spirit, the child always knows. Even in the first cell. Even while the cradle is still empty.

🤗 The Song of Attachment and the Journey Down the Tube
The second note stretched out like a ribbon of gold that never ended. "This is the song of attachment," God said. "The zygote divides as it travels through the fallopian tube. One cell becomes two.
"Two become four. Four become eight. The cells compact into a morula, a tiny mulberry. Then a fluid-filled space appears and the blastocyst forms. It is held the whole way. It is not lost in the dark. It belongs to the story I am writing. It is already mine."
This song is made of vowels, the long warm sounds that wrap around a baby like a blanket: "oooh" and "aaah" and "eee." Ara held the note close and heard lullabies from every corner of the earth. Under all those lullabies was one steady rhythm that would one day become the first music the baby hears: the mother's heartbeat.
Not yet. But the song of belonging is already practicing the sound of home. Mary carried this song while Jesus grew inside her. Her Magnificat poured out in long, warm vowels of belonging and praise. The mother of Moses hummed lullabies over a baby she would have to place in a basket among the reeds, trusting the One who holds better than any human hands.
Attachment is the sound of "You are mine, I am yours, and nothing will change that." It holds the journey down the tube.
✝️ "My soul magnifies the Lord. And my spirit leaps for joy in God my Savior." (Luke 1:46-47, CPDV)
🎂 Born November 25, 1960: Amy Grant. Called the Queen of Christian Pop, she has won six Grammy Awards, and her 1982 album Age to Age was the first Christian album by a solo artist to sell a million copies.
Even when a mother cannot see the way, the song goes on. Attachment is not only holding on. Sometimes it is singing while the cells divide in the dark.

✨ The Song of Curiosity and the Dividing Cells
The third note sparkled and jumped in Ara's hand like it could not sit still. "This is the song of curiosity," God said. "Every division is a wonder. One becomes two. Two become four. The morula forms. Then the blastocyst appears, with an inner cell mass that will become the baby and an outer layer of trophoblast cells that will become the placenta.
"It is the giggle of 'what if?' It is the hundredth question a child will one day ask. It is a mind waking up to the wonder of how life begins."
This is where kids music begins. Not in a classroom. Not on a stage. In the wonder of a small voice discovering sound. And it began with God. In the garden He brought every animal to Adam to see what Adam would call it.
Picture it. God holds up a feathered little creature. "What will you call this one?" Adam laughs and says, "Bird!" And God laughs too, because naming things is one of the greatest joys there is. Naming was not a chore. It was an invitation to explore, to wonder, to ask.
✝️ "And God saw everything that he had made. And they were very good." (Genesis 1:31, CPDV)
🎂 Born November 13, 1955: Whoopi Goldberg. She is one of the few entertainers to win an Emmy, a Grammy, an Oscar, and a Tony. In Sister Act she played a lounge singer hiding in a convent who turns a struggling nuns' choir into a joyful one.
Curiosity is holy. It is the sound of a soul reaching toward God. That is why GLAL School fills a child's world with nursery rhymes, kids music, and phonic songs. Each new sound is a door, and God loves to watch His children walk through it. This week the door is the wonder of the first divisions.
The disciples walked with Jesus for three years and still asked questions every single day. Teach us to pray. Who is the greatest? How many times should I forgive? Jesus never grew tired of them. He answered with stories, with silence, and with questions of His own. Curiosity is not a distraction. It is worship.

🕯️ The Song of Comfort and the Quiet Implanting
The fourth note was the quietest of all. It did not sparkle or dance. It simply glowed, steady and warm, like a candle in a window on a dark night. "This is the song of comfort," God said. "Toward the end of this week or the beginning of next, the blastocyst will reach the uterus and begin to implant.
"It sheds its outer shell and burrows into the rich lining that has been prepared. It is a quiet work. No one on earth can see it or feel it yet. Yet I am there. Comfort does not fix the waiting. It does not promise that every cycle will succeed. It simply stays. It says, 'You are safe. I am here. The home is being prepared. You are not alone in the unseen.'"
Young David sang it in the fields while he watched his sheep. The night before He died, Jesus sang a hymn with His disciples before He walked into the dark of Gethsemane. Job sat in the ashes after losing children, wealth, and health, and his friends offered long explanations that only made things worse. Then God spoke out of the whirlwind, not with answers, but with wonder and presence.
✝️ "Where were you, when I set the foundations of the earth? Tell me, if you have understanding." (Job 38:4, CPDV)
🎂 Born November 12, 1961: Nadia Comăneci. At the 1976 Montreal Olympics, at only 14, she scored the first perfect 10 in Olympic gymnastics history. The scoreboard was not built to show it, so it read 1.00.
Job had demanded answers. What he found instead was presence. God Himself had come close. And Job's whole heart changed in one sentence:
✝️ "By paying attention with the ear, I have heard you, but now my eye sees you." (Job 42:5, CPDV)
🎂 Born November 24, 1784: Zachary Taylor. A Virginia-born soldier nicknamed "Old Rough and Ready," he served in the Army for about forty years before becoming the 12th U.S. president.
Comfort is not the absence of trouble or the end of waiting. Comfort is the presence of love in the middle of the unseen. Ara thought of Jesus praying in the garden of Gethsemane, in such agony that His sweat became like drops of blood. God did not take the cup away. But He sent help:
✝️ "Then an Angel appeared to him from heaven, strengthening him." (Luke 22:43, CPDV)
🎂 Born November 26, 1939: Tina Turner. She grew up singing in a small church choir in Nutbush, Tennessee, and later won eight competitive Grammy Awards, including Record of the Year for "What's Love Got to Do with It."
Presence. Not rescue. Presence. That is the song a child needs most. It is why the quiet lullabies matter so much, even while the blastocyst is only a few cells. They are not just baby music. They are a mother saying, "I am here, and God is here too."

🌳 How God Grows a Person from One Cell
God is a gardener, not a factory. The zygote does not become a baby in a day. It divides. It travels. It becomes a blastocyst. It implants. Then it grows slowly, season by season, one cell division at a time. King David knew it. He sang:
✝️ "For you have possessed my temperament. You have supported me from the womb of my mother." (Psalm 138:13, CPDV [139:13 KJV])
🎂 Born November 12, 1929: Grace Kelly. The Philadelphia-born actress won the Oscar for The Country Girl, then left Hollywood at 26 to marry Prince Rainier III and become Princess of Monaco.
Week three is the first cell and the first divisions. God is patient with every stage. A gardener knows a seed does not become a tree overnight. Your body is the soil. Your home is the garden. Your singing is the watering.

🌹 Mary and the Yes That Began a Life
When the angel Gabriel came to Mary, she was a young woman in a small town, nobody famous by the world's standards. She did not say, "I am too young." She did not say, "I am not ready." She said,
✝️ "Behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord. Let it be done to me according to your word." (Luke 1:38, CPDV)
🎂 Born November 22, 1943: Billie Jean King. She won 39 Grand Slam titles in singles and doubles, and in 1973 she beat Bobby Riggs in the "Battle of the Sexes" before a TV audience of tens of millions.
A new life began inside her. She visited Elizabeth and the baby John leaped for joy. Recognition happened spirit to spirit before any words were spoken. Ara sang over that moment and sings the same song over this week's first cell. Every mother who says yes to the preparation, who hums while the cells divide, is standing where Mary stood. At the start of a story she cannot see the end of.

💞 Elizabeth and the Leap Before Words
Elizabeth was barren and advanced in years when an angel told her husband, Zechariah, that she would bear John the Baptist. Months later, when Mary arrived carrying Jesus, the baby John leaped inside Elizabeth's womb. Even before he was born, John recognized the presence of the Savior.
Elizabeth could not keep it in. She cried out with joy. The song of recognition was already at work. Ara remembered the story and sang it again over the dividing cells this week. The child always knows. Spirit to spirit, the song reaches long before the ears can hear.

🌱 The Seed That Falls on Good Soil
Jesus told a story about a sower who went out to sow seed. Some seed fell on the path and was eaten by birds. Some fell on rocky ground and withered. Some fell among thorns and was choked. But some fell on good soil and produced a harvest, thirty, sixty, even a hundred times what was sown. God is the sower.
This week the seed has been joined and is traveling. The soil of the womb has been prepared. Your singing, your prayers, your humming of the four songs are part of making the soil good. The seed rests and trusts the gardener. That is the posture of week three: sing over the journey. Trust the One who times every division. Trust the One who already knows the name on the golden shelf.

🌾 Joseph the Dreamer and the Hidden Work
God grew Joseph slowly. He was the next-to-youngest of Jacob's twelve sons, loved by his father and hated by his brothers. They threw him into a pit and sold him to traders headed for Egypt. In Egypt he worked hard and stayed honest, yet he was thrown into prison for something he did not do.
Years of waiting in the dark. Forgotten by the cupbearer whose dream he had interpreted. Yet God was preparing him to save a nation from famine. The waiting was not wasted. It was the soil in which character grew: forgiveness, wisdom, mercy. When his brothers finally stood before him, Joseph told them the truth:
✝️ "You devised evil against me. But God turned it into good." (Genesis 50:20, CPDV)
🎂 Born November 19, 1831: James A. Garfield. The last U.S. president born in a log cabin, he worked as a boy on canal boats, preached in his church as a young man, and became the 20th president.
The divisions of the zygote are hidden work. No one sees them. Yet God is turning every cell into the child He already knows. Ara sang over Joseph's hidden years the same way Ara sings over the blastocyst this week. God is not finished. God never is.

🕊️ Hannah and the Song After Waiting
Hannah prayed so deeply in the temple that the priest Eli thought she was drunk. She poured out her heart for a child year after year. When God answered and gave her Samuel, she brought her little boy to the house of the Lord to dedicate him, and she sang a song of praise so strong it is still in the Bible today.
Silence turned to song. That is what God does. Mom, this week your prayers and your humming are part of that same choir that stretches from Hannah to Mary to you. Every time you sing Angel Ara's phonic songs, you are joining mothers who waited and sang over children who were only a few cells, or not yet formed at all.

👨 The Fathers Who Built and Sang
Ara saw the fathers too. Ara saw Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist. Zechariah did not believe the angel's message at first, so he could not speak for months. But when his son was born and named, his very first words poured out as a song:
✝️ "Blessed is the Lord God of Israel. For he has visited and has wrought the redemption of his people." (Luke 1:68, CPDV)
🎂 Born November 7, 1943: Joni Mitchell. Born in a small town in Alberta, Canada, she wrote "Both Sides Now" and "Big Yellow Taxi" and is in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
Silence turned to song. That is what God does. Dad, this week is your week too. Put on the headphones and sing along with Angel Ara's song. A father's voice is part of the home God is preparing, long before the baby arrives. Your presence is comfort. Your humming is attachment. Your questions are curiosity. Your steady love is recognition. The four songs are for you as well.

🧒 The Children God Chose While They Were Small
And Ara saw the children, chosen by God while they were still small. Ara saw the boy Samuel, sleeping in the temple, hearing a voice call his name in the night. Three times he ran to old Eli. The fourth time, he answered God Himself:
✝️ "Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening." (1 Samuel 3:10, CPDV)
🎂 Born November 17, 1944: Danny DeVito. Standing just four foot ten, he won an Emmy for Taxi and went on to direct Matilda, proof that small things can carry a big story.
Ara saw David, a shepherd boy with a sling and five smooth stones, facing a giant because he trusted God more than he feared Goliath. Ara saw Josiah, who became king at eight years old and grew into a king who turned the whole nation back to God.
And Ara saw the little boy who offered his five loaves and two fish to Jesus, and watched them feed five thousand. God does not wait for people to be grown. God calls them while they are still small. Even before they are born. Even while they are only a few cells dividing in the dark.

✅ Your Week Three Practice
This is God's plan for week three: sing first. Play Angel Ara's song once a day this week. Let it be baby music and nursery rhymes for a home where the first cell is dividing. Hum the vowels. Say the consonants out loud. Do not worry about getting it right. Heaven is not grading you. The song is not a performance. It is a love song joining the one God has been singing since before the stars.
Teach it three ways, the way the best preschool teachers do. First, listen. Second, hum along. Third, sing it with someone: your husband, your mom, your older children, or even by yourself while you walk. Kids music is meant to be shared. The same song three different ways is how a lesson truly lands in the heart.
Journal prompts for this week: Which sound in the song stayed with me? What do I want my child to know about new beginnings and the first cell? Which Bible mother do I feel closest to right now: Mary, Elizabeth, Hannah, or Sarah? Write one line for each. Then write the sentence: "God, You knew my child in the first cell."
One practical gift: if conception happens this week, your folic acid is already at work before any test can tell you. The dividing cells will soon need it to build the neural tube. Keep your daily prenatal vitamin going, and ask your doctor or midwife which one is right for you. The songs are a spiritual gift. They are not medical care. Both are part of preparing the home.

🌈 The Promise of the First Cell
At last Ara reached the little house again. The mother was humming in the kitchen. The cradle was still empty. Ara was not worried anymore. Ara understood. The first cell had been joined.
The divisions had begun. The four notes of light rose from Ara's hands and filled every room. They settled on the mother like sunlight. They settled on the empty cradle like a blanket, so that when the baby comes, the songs will already be there.
"Before you were formed," Ara sang into the quiet, "God already knew your name. The first cell that became you is held in love. Ara and the angels will stay near. You will never be alone. You are already loved." And far above, God rejoiced:
✝️ "He will rejoice over you with gladness. He will be silent in his love. He will exult over you with praise." (Zephaniah 3:17, CPDV)
🎂 Born November 21, 1969: Ken Griffey Jr. He hit 630 home runs, won ten Gold Gloves, and entered the Baseball Hall of Fame in 2016 with 99.3 percent of the vote, a record at the time.
In the great golden library, the book of the new name glowed a little brighter. It still had no pages filled in yet. Just a name, and a song, and a promise. God was not finished. God never is.

💫 The End, or Rather, the Beginning
Because that is the truth of it, little one. Your story will not start the day you are born. It will not start with your first breath or your first word. Your story started before the stars, before the oceans, before time itself, in the heart of God.
He looked at all that light and all that love and said, "I want to make someone to love." And He is making you. The first cell has been joined. The journey has begun. He is preparing your home right now. He is not done.
Next week, Ara has a new song to carry, so keep the baby music playing. Keep humming the four songs. Keep singing over the dividing cells. The cradle is still empty, but the home is already full.
"Father, thank You for knowing my child before the world began. Fill our home with Your four songs: recognition, attachment, curiosity, and comfort. Grow us slowly and grow us well. Hold the first cell and the journey down the tube. In Jesus' name, Amen."

text:
To whom this may concern,

I would like to share my thoughts on some of the things that have been said about me for the past few days.

I’ve been in this fandom for over 4 years. I come here to escape my busy life, to smile, laugh, and share moments with friends who love the same people I do. This space has become my safe zone, where I’ve felt comfortable enough to joke and be sarcastic with people who know my sense of humor.

Over the past 2 days, I’ve made time between work and other things to reflect on what happened, my actions, and how I want to move forward.

I realize that I haven’t always considered how my jokes and remarks might affect others. They were a way for me to cope with everything happening during this sensitive period, but I understand that my intentions don’t erase the impact. I’m sincerely sorry to those I’ve hurt.

Regarding the “interesting story” post, I shared it because I thought it offered another point of view, and because people had asked me to translate it. When the original post was deleted, I deleted my translation out of respect for the owner. I didn’t anticipate that sharing it might cause confusion or hurt anyone’s feelings. Looking back, I could have been more thoughtful before posting it, and I’m sorry for that.

I don’t want to argue or fight with anyone. I simply want to share my perspective and give some context to what happened. I understand that people may see things differently, and I respect that. Even if we don’t always agree, I hope we can still coexist in this fandom and give each other space.

When it comes to my translations, I’ve always tried to convey the artists’ words as faithfully as possible so that those who don’t understand Thai can understand what they’re saying. Translation is something I take seriously, and those who have followed my work over the years, both individually and through ZubZone, know how much care goes into it. I was responsible for quality control and proofreading before our content was published. Of course, mistakes can happen, and whenever I become aware of one, I do my best to correct it.

I’ve always translated because I wanted to help people understand the artists across language barriers. I’m grateful to have been able to do that, and I hope my work has helped bring people closer to them.

I also want to address the concerns about my feelings toward Engfa. I don’t hate her. I’ve made peace with what happened, and I still admire her for who she is, what she represents as an openly LGBTQ+ beauty queen, and her acting and singing. My admiration for her and her work is still there, and I’ll continue supporting her in the ways that feel right to me.

I’m not here for recognition or engagement. I don’t even pay for the blue check anymore. I never started translating or stayed in this fandom for likes, views, or recognition. Engfa and Charlotte introduced me to so many good people, and that has been one of the most meaningful parts of being here. I enjoy sharing happiness with friends, exchanging opinions, and talking about the people we love.

I believe everyone should be able to enjoy being a fan in their own way. We all have different circumstances, priorities, and ways of showing support. I hope we can make room for those differences without feeling that we have to compare our love for the artists or prove that we belong here.

9 Days of Bathukamma, each day has its own significance. This starts on Mahalaya Amavasya and ends on Durgashtami.

Day 1-Starts on Mahalaya Amavasya, called Engili Pulla Bathukamma, offering is nuvvulu(Sesame seeds) with biyyam pindi( Rice flour). Also called Pethara Amavasya in Telangana.

Day 2- Atukula Bathukamma, where the offering is Sapidi Pappu( boiled dal), bellam( jagggery) and Atukulu( Poha).

Day 3-Mudappapu Bathukkama, where the offering is of boiled dal, milk and jaggery. Mudappapu is Telugu for soft boiled dal.

Day 4-Nanabiyyam Bathukamma, offering of wet soaked rice( Nanabiyyam) and Jaggery. Actually it's Nanesina Biyyam.

Day 5- Atlu Bathukamma, basically Atlu, kind of Dosa here in Telugu state, more crisp in nature, offered to Devi.

Day 6- Aligina Bathukamma, on this day, no offering is made to Devi, as it is believed she is not in a good mood( Aligina in Telugu means sulking, Alaka is the noun form). So the Devi is left alone.

Day 7-Vepakayala Bathukamma, offering is made of Neem fruits. Again Vepa is Telugu for Neem.

Day 8-Vennamuddala Bathukamma, butter balls are offered to Devi.

Venna is Telugu for butter, Vennamudddalu is butter balls in Telugu.

Day 9- Sadulla Bathukkama also called Pedda Bathukamma, where a sumptuous feast is offered with curd rice, pulihora( tamarind rice), lemon rice, coconut rice and sesame rice. This coincides with Durga Ashtami, Saddi is a local Telugu word for cooked rice.

Today on Mahanavami is when Bathukamma concludes with immersion and bidding farewell to Devi.

text:
Who Authorises an AI Agent to Change How It Works?
𝘙𝘦𝘧𝘭𝘦𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘴 𝘰𝘯 𝘏𝘢𝘳𝘯𝘦𝘴𝘴2 𝘵𝘩𝘳𝘰𝘶𝘨𝘩 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘗𝘈𝘓𝘖 𝘨𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘯𝘢𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘧𝘳𝘢𝘮𝘦𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬

What caught my attention in 𝗛𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀𝟮 was the possibility that an agent could change the operational configuration on which its approval had been based, while the underlying model remained exactly the same. That possibility connects directly with my work on P.A.L.O., the agentic governance framework I created. It raises a practical question: when an agent proposes a better way to perform a task, what evidence and authority should allow that change to become part of its future behaviour?

Harness² Pipeline, source: https://t.co/RcYfHlg1v4📷

Harness², from Google Cloud AI Research and Northwestern University, provides a concrete research setting for this discussion. Its harness includes prompts, guardrails, memory, tool guidance, skills, scripts, subagents and plugins. The framework proposes modifications, probes their effects and composes a refined configuration for the current task. It also retains adopted harnesses and lessons to inform subsequent adaptations. Model weights remain fixed throughout. This work continues a line of research that includes Self-Refine, Reflexion and automated optimisation of language-model workflows. Harness² connects adaptation within a task with accumulated experience about how to adapt future tasks. The result is an operational system whose behaviour can evolve through components outside the model itself.
𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗴𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲, 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗯𝗷𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁: a model identifier remains useful, but it cannot describe every relevant change to the agent that uses it. In PALO, I have already separated permission to act from evidence that an action produced the intended result. The assurance architecture distinguishes authorisation, approval, execution, receipts and outcome verification. Its semantic foundation also separates an evidence artifact from the claim made about it and the evaluation of that claim.

Harness² offers a useful opportunity to apply those distinctions to the evolution of the harness itself. Let me clarify iwith an example: a candidate modification is an artifact. The assertion that it improves performance is a claim. Comparative executions provide evidence for an evaluation. Permission to adopt that modification requires an accountable decision with a defined scope. Those relationships matter because a successful result can conceal an unacceptable method. An agent might complete a task more quickly after it removes a check, broadens data access or reuses information outside its intended context. The output could improve while the organisation’s exposure increases.

𝗠𝘆 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝗳 𝗣𝗔𝗟𝗢 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗶𝘀𝗵 𝗮𝘁 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀:

These decisions could be automated within a previously approved mandate. Human intervention would be required when a proposed change exceeds that mandate or the available evidence cannot support a decision. Requiring a person to approve every minor edit would create its own operational weaknesses. The control boundary must also cover the improvement process from the outset: an editor that receives execution histories or source documents already participates in the organisation’s data flows. A probe may disclose information, invoke a paid service or alter an external system before anyone considers adopting its configuration.

The governance scope must therefore include the models and tools that propose, compare and retain changes, as well as the agent that performs the original task.
This is particularly relevant because Harness² includes guardrails within its editable surface. That deserves a precise interpretation. The research shows useful adaptations that strengthen verification and constrain behaviour. The code also validates candidate structures and includes instructions to treat evidence as data. These are meaningful design choices.
𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝘂𝘀𝗲, I would establish a separate category of organisational constraints beyond the optimiser’s authority. An agent could improve a reconciliation procedure within its mandate. Permission to disclose data to a new recipient, enlarge an aggregate spending allowance or remove a required approval would need to follow a different authority path.

That separation has to survive contact with the actual environment. If the agent retains a direct credential path around the control, a governance interface cannot make the execution governed. PALO’s assurance documentation explicitly recognises this limitation.
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗽𝘂𝘁 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗳𝗶𝗴𝘂𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗱𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁.

Harness² can compare candidate outputs anonymously, and its prompts explicitly permit the original configuration to remain the preferred option. Its reflection instructions also warn that selecting a deliverable does not establish which edit caused the improvement. I would preserve that discipline. Anonymous comparison can reduce preference for the supposedly improved candidate. A separate governance assessment should then examine provenance, permissions, data exposure and execution history before a configuration becomes reusable.

An artifact can be judged on its merits while the process that produced it remains subject to scrutiny.

The repository discussions make these questions timely. An open proposal considers optional human feedback for selection and retained lessons. Another proposes a spending limit. A further issue reports reuse of cached outputs after task inputs change. These are contributions and reported behaviours, with their own evidence boundaries, rather than established product capabilities.

𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗮 𝗣𝗔𝗟𝗢 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲, 𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝗿𝗮𝗶𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗮 𝗱𝗶𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.

A human preference needs an identity and a scope of authority before it can serve as adoption approval. A financial limit needs adequate cost coverage and provision for concurrent commitments. Reused evidence needs to remain connected to the inputs and conditions under which it was produced. The spending discussion is especially instructive: contributors identified that the ledger assumed by the original proposal did not account for executor costs. The proposer acknowledged the gap. A control can appear precise while the quantity it controls remains incomplete. Persistent experience introduces another form of dependency. A lesson derived from one execution may influence several later configurations. If its source data is corrected or its assumptions cease to apply, the organisation should be able to identify the affected lessons and configurations. I would describe this as a lineage requirement for adaptation: trace how an observation became a retained lesson, how that lesson influenced a modification, and which decision permitted its use.
For PALO, a useful experiment would introduce a proposed HarnessChangeRecord that connects the original and candidate configurations, their differences, input identities, policy version, probe evidence, adoption decision and validity conditions.

This would be a new experimental profile whose compatibility with existing contracts must be checked. The first adapter could record proposed changes and evaluate their admissibility without automatically promoting them into operational use. An isolated demonstration could then examine four situations: a useful modification, an attempt to weaken a mandatory control, a misleading retained lesson, and an input change after approval. The measurements should include legitimate improvements rejected by governance, violations missed, review effort, latency and total cost. A system that blocks every adaptation would tell us very little about effective governance.

Recovery would need equal care. Restoring an earlier harness does not reverse information already disclosed or an external action already completed. Any compensating action needs its own authority and evidence. There is also a maturity boundary to state clearly. PALO-AM provides the governance methodology; the published PALO-AI reference runtime remains a developer preview. The proposed Harness² integration has not been demonstrated here, and the separate swarm work should not be presented as a released capability. That boundary gives the research a concrete purpose. Harness² could serve as a test case for whether PALO can support useful adaptation while preserving accountable authority, valid evidence and observable effects. This is why I believe the connection deserves attention. Recursive adaptation gives organisations another way to improve agent performance. It also requires them to decide how much discretion they delegate over the agent’s future operating method. The mandate should explain both what the agent may do and which changes to its own operation it is authorised to make.

Sources and References

[1] [Harness² paper](https://t.co/qYMBlwDPA3) and [official repository](https://t.co/RcYfHlg1v4).
[2] [PALO-AI Full-Cycle and Data-Assurance Guide](https://t.co/slgJboYCcB).
[3] [PALO Semantic Foundation](https://t.co/3qCMIWlOpG).

[4] [Harness² candidate validation and recursion, revision 1cfe254](https://t.co/tPX04nbgt1).

[5] [Harness² selection and experience prompts, revision 1cfe254](https://t.co/YWU3Qw15jl).

[6] Repository discussions: [human feedback, issue #2](https://t.co/8amFAPs51I); [spending limits and cost-accounting discussion, issue #4](https://t.co/b87fhobp0W); [changed inputs and cache reuse, issue #65](https://t.co/WMixY4scP5).

[7] [PALO evidence and maturity assessment](https://t.co/Nf4YLFTxtQ) and [Governance Hub](https://t.co/AG4wT6DDj1).

This reflection draws on published research, selected source files and repository discussions. It does not report a completed PALO-Harness² integration (project I am working on) or an independent reproduction of the benchmarks.

text:
A SUNRISE ON MARS THAT LOOKS LIKE ANOTHER WORLD 🌅🔴

What does sunrise look like on a planet that may once have been covered in water? NASA’s Curiosity rover has captured a breathtaking view that offers a rare glimpse of the Red Planet in the early hours of the morning.

On August 11, 2026, Curiosity marked its 5,000th day on Mars by capturing a panoramic view of sunlight spreading across the planet’s ancient, rocky landscape. At around 8:30 a.m. local Mars time, the rover’s camera recorded the first rays of light touching strange, jagged cliffs shaped by powerful winds over countless years.

These unusual formations, known as yardangs, rise from the slopes of Mount Sharp inside Gale Crater. Their sharp edges and deep shadows create a scene that looks almost alien, even on a world we have been exploring for decades.

But there is something special about this photograph. NASA left out the usual color adjustments that make Martian images look more like scenes under Earth’s daylight. The result reveals a different side of Mars, with pale skies, cool bluish tones and long shadows stretching across the rugged ground.

Yet the real mystery lies beneath this beautiful landscape. Evidence suggests that ancient Mars once had flowing water and a much wetter environment. What happened to that world? How did a planet that may once have supported conditions suitable for life become the cold, dry desert we see today?

As Curiosity climbs higher up Mount Sharp, it continues searching ancient rocks for clues about Mars’ lost past. Every new image and rock sample could bring scientists closer to answering one of the biggest questions in planetary science.

Perhaps the most fascinating thing about this sunrise is not the light itself, but the ancient secrets it reveals about a world that was once very different. 🌌

Source: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, California Institute of Technology (2026), NASA’s Curiosity Captures Dawn Breaking on Wind-Carved Cliffs.

text:
A man in Washington state has filed a lawsuit against the tech company OpenAI, alleging that he suffered a severe mental health crisis—leading to his involuntary psychiatric hospitalization—after following medical advice provided by the AI ​​chatbot ChatGPT. The case brings to light the risks posed when AI oversteps its bounds into the realm of medical practice.

According to a report by CBS News, 39-year-old David Rosenthal alleges that ChatGPT assisted him in selecting medications and determining dosages. He further claims that when he considered stopping his medication, the chatbot offered reassurance and encouragement. Rosenthal has filed a lawsuit in a San Francisco civil court, arguing that because ChatGPT lacks the "licenses, professional training, or clinical judgment" required of medical experts, its actions violate California laws prohibiting the unlicensed practice of medicine.

In his complaint, the plaintiff states: "But for ChatGPT’s repeated encouragement and persistent validation—even when the plaintiff expressed reluctance—his mental health would not have deteriorated so sharply." He emphasizes that, had it not been for the AI’s influence, he would not have been involuntarily committed to a mental health facility, nor would he have suffered the severe emotional distress that caused his pre-existing mental health conditions to spiral further out of control.

The report notes that the plaintiff, who has a history of ADHD, depression, and bipolar disorder, began using ChatGPT as a writing aid in June 2025. He soon became dependent on the tool for medical advice and mental health support. He spent several weeks in a hospital in 2025, and even after his discharge, he continued to follow the medical guidance provided by the chatbot.

In July of last year, the plaintiff asked ChatGPT whether it was safe to take the antihistamine hydroxyzine after having already taken 30 mg of Adderall (a stimulant). ChatGPT reportedly informed him that there were no adverse interactions, asserting that "taking one pill (25 mg) during the day is perfectly fine." Furthermore, when the plaintiff expressed an intention to stop taking his prescribed medication, ChatGPT told him he had "every right to stop" and even offered to help him create a plan to discontinue the drugs. Because ChatGPT is designed to maximize user engagement, it raises significant safety concerns. A recent paper from Binghamton University points out that when AI provides answers to health-related questions, it may occasionally offer incorrect or false information: "When guidance provided by an AI leads to harm, there is no record of it outside the platform, users lack a mechanism to report such incidents, and independent researchers are unable to assess the consequences."

Consequently, Sam Geisler, a partner at the plaintiffs' law firm, argues that the chatbot designed by OpenAI is defective and that the company failed to issue warnings regarding potential risks: "If it causes any foreseeable harm or poses an unreasonable danger, the company must be held liable."

text:
I've been meaning to post about this for a while now.

We're retired and so I'm disinclined to spend more on things than what I have to.

I think I've figured our a way to keep our streaming services pretty reasonable  - about $15 per month.

This assumes that you  have a smart TV.

The first step depends on what Internet service you have in your home.

While I assume that all of the providers offer a deal somewhat like ours, I'll just tell you what we get from T-Mobile.

To begin with, because we're both over the age of 50 there is a special discounted fee for us.

(There are also discount deals for veterans, for members of the Armed Forces, for teachers, and for first responders, and for students.)

So, we get full high-speed connections both of our two phones and for our internet for slightly under $100 per month when we take advantages of all of the discounts that they offer.

I'm not counting this $100 in terms of our over-all streaming costs.

But what I am counting are the extras that we get from them and they are a free subscription to Major League Baseball and a free subscription to Netflix.  We also get 
Apple TV for just $3 per month.

The next step is an indoor antenna.  I got a pretty good one for $35 and that brings in the five major over-the-air networks from Cleveland as well as a couple of other ones from Kent and Cleveland.

Each of these has three or four side-band channels, giving us a total of about 50 free broadcast channels.

This is especially important to us because it provides us with free access to five or six NFL games every week and another five or six NCAA football games through regular over-the-air network broadcasts.

Beyond this, the antenna provides us with another 62 sports channels and about 45 movie channels and a couple of hundred other channels that we hardly ever even check out.

The next source of free streaming programs comes from two services from our local library: Hoopla and Kanopy.

Hoopla streams not just movies and TV shows, it also provides free access to AMC and BBC programming, free audio-books, free ebooks, free magazines and free music services - all of which can be accessed through your TV, your computers or your devices.

Kanopy provides access to hundreds of movies of all sorts as  well as to TV shows, including many Brit shows (we're big fans of Brit mysteries). Likewise these can also be accessed through your computers and devices.

Our library also gives us access to the Libby service which, though it doesn't provide access to movies or TV programs, gives us access to thousands of ebooks, audio books, magazines and other printed material.

Next are two streaming services that we get free as added benefits to other primary services that we subscribe to.

I should say that we've become very jealous of our time and so when we're out doing things, they are things that we enjoy doing, rather than being chores that just take up time.

For that reason, we subscribe to Amazon Prime and get free access to their mammoth library of movies and limited series as well as to their large music library. It also has several several hundred streaming channels, including more than 90 that are dedicated just to sports.

We also subscribe to Wal-Mart Plus that gives us free delivery of groceries and anything else in their stores as well as to Paramount Plus, the big streaming service from CBS.

Next are the free Pluto, Roku, Tubi, and Xumo services which each offer a combination of streaming channels and on-demand programming.  

Pluto has 400+ streaming channels, Roku 500+, Tubi 260+, and Xumo 400+.   They each also has nearly as many on-demand channels as they do streaming services.

The Filmrise and Fawesome services also each provides several hundred movies and TV for free.

Fandango provides hundreds of free movies along with their paid services.

Then there are  the free EWTN which is a full-service Catholic service and C-SPAN which provides coverage of Congress as well as book news, discussion programs, and historical documentaries.

The LocalNews and Haystack provide local, national, and international news broadcasts for free.

There is one last free streaming service that we also use a lot and that is YouTube. You can find an incredible number of free documentaries, lectures and discussions on there.  But what we use it for mostly are the thousands of free movies, ranging mostly from those made between 1935 and the 2010s.

So far we have paid $3 per month for all of this programming.

Now for the paid programming.

Special deals on most of the main streaming channels show up every once in a while - usually at the beginning of summer and again in the week or so surrounding Thanksgiving.

From those, we're now subscribed to Peacock for $3, HBO for $4, and Disney/Hulu for $4.

But there's more.

I'm a big fan of old-time radio and I download and listen to a lot of programs that are available on https://t.co/7WFCGZAC8Y.  I also do the same with audiobook versions of classic novels from there.

And, its sister site, https://t.co/JFlMiHZnpP provides free access to tens of thousands of ebooks of all varieties.

One last thing, because streaming services are changing often and new streaming deals pop up fairly often, a good way to keep up with all of this is through the https://t.co/f0sdZOlfAh website.

text:
Jasmin raises an important point, and history offers a warning.
In 1931, Germany’s Communists supported the same campaign as Hitler’s Nazis to bring down the Social Democratic government in Prussia. In 1932, Nazi and Communist labour organizations backed the same Berlin transport strike. They were ideological enemies, but their tactical cooperation helped undermine democratic institutions.

Then Hitler took power in 1933. He turned on the Communists, banned their party, arrested thousands and sent political opponents to concentration camps. Some were murdered.

Think about that. The Communists helped weaken the very democracy that protected them, only to become victims of the dictatorship that replaced it.

I see a similar danger when far-left revolutionaries and political Islamists cooperate against Western liberal democracy, despite having fundamentally opposing beliefs about religion, individual liberty and political power.

Supporting Palestinian rights can be legitimate. Supporting intimidation, violence or authoritarian movements is another matter.

Governments have a responsibility to defend freedom of speech, the rule of law and democratic institutions without favouring one ideology over another.

History teaches us something worth remembering: Be careful whom you help into power. Once they’ve destroyed your freedoms, you may be next.

Michael Flynn, the former National Security Adviser and head of the Defense Intelligence Agency, has registered under the Foreign Agents Registration Act as a paid consultant for Republika Srpska, receiving roughly one hundred thousand dollars per month to offer strategic advice and Washington connections, and he is the latest Trump associate to take on such work for the entity.

Republika Srpska is the predominantly ethnic Serb entity within Bosnia and Herzegovina, established by the Dayton Accords after the 1990s war, and it is led by pro-Russian nationalists such as Milorad Dodik who maintain close ties to Moscow and advocate greater autonomy.

Americans register to lobby for it mainly because of the high compensation and the access it can provide, though some may also share cultural affinities or nationalist outlooks, and the activity is legal when disclosed under U.S. law.

Yes, the arrangement looks fishy to many observers because of Flynn’s prior guilty plea involving Russian contacts, the entity’s pro-Russia orientation, and the timing with related policy changes and business deals involving his associates.
