Let’s talk current events. Since Putin took presidency 25 years ago 
Chechnya (Second Chechen War): A Prelude to Expansionism
While the First Chechen War predates Putin’s rise to power, the Second Chechen War, beginning in 1999 and intensifying under Putin’s leadership, offered an early indication of his approach to territorial integrity and security. Officially framed as an anti-terrorist operation to suppress separatists, the conflict resulted in widespread destruction and human rights abuses.
•The brutal tactics employed in Chechnya set a precedent for subsequent military actions.
•The war consolidated Putin’s image as a strong leader willing to use force to protect Russian interests.
Georgia (2008): A Foray into the Near Abroad
The 2008 Russo-Georgian War marked a significant escalation in Russia’s willingness to project military power beyond its borders. Russia intervened in support of separatist movements in South Ossetia and Abkhazia, both internationally recognized as part of Georgia.
•Pretext: Russia claimed it was protecting its citizens (many of whom had been granted Russian passports) from Georgian aggression.
•Outcome: Russia recognized the independence of South Ossetia and Abkhazia, establishing a military presence in both regions and further undermining Georgian sovereignty. The invasion highlighted Russia’s willingness to disregard international norms and territorial integrity. This action definitively placed Georgia on the list of countries which has Putin invaded.
Ukraine (2014-Present): A Protracted Conflict and Annexation of Crimea
The situation in Ukraine represents the most prolonged and extensive example of Russian military intervention under Putin. The conflict began in 2014, following the Maidan Revolution, which ousted the pro-Russian Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych.
•Annexation of Crimea (2014):Russia seized and annexed the Crimean Peninsula, a region with a majority-Russian population. This was widely condemned as a violation of international law.
•Support for Separatists in Donbas (2014-2022): Russia provided military, financial, and political support to separatist groups in eastern Ukraine’s Donbas region, fueling a protracted conflict that resulted in thousands of casualties.
•Full-Scale Invasion (2022-Present): In February 2022, Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, significantly escalating the conflict and resulting in widespread devastation and displacement. The invasion has been met with near-universal condemnation and unprecedented international sanctions. Russia’s actions have undeniably confirmed Ukraine as one of the countries which has Putin invaded.
Syria (2015-Present): Intervention Beyond the Former Soviet Sphere
While not a direct invasion in the same sense as Georgia or Ukraine, Russia’s military intervention in Syria, starting in 2015, represents another significant projection of Russian power under Putin. This intervention was at the request of the Syrian government to support President Bashar al-Assad.
•Justification: Russia claimed its involvement was aimed at combating terrorism, specifically ISIS.
•Impact: Russian military support has been crucial in helping the Assad regime regain control over much of Syria. The intervention has also been accompanied by allegations of human rights abuses and indiscriminate targeting of civilian areas. While framed differently, the Syrian intervention showcased Putin’s willingness to use military force to achieve Russia’s strategic objectives, even outside its immediate neighborhood.
Moldova (Ongoing Political Interference and Military Presence)
While not a full-scale military invasion, Moldova experiences ongoing political interference and has a Russian military presence in Transnistria, a breakaway region bordering Ukraine. The situation in Transnistria predates Putin, but the Russian military presence there serves as a constant source of tension and contributes to Moldova’s instability.

5. Geopolitical implications
The project has implications beyond shipbuilding.
For Washington: It offers an opportunity to reinforce allied industrial supply chains, increase maritime maintenance options and establish alternatives to excessive concentration of strategic infrastructure.
For Athens: It could strengthen Greece's position as a regional logistics, shipbuilding and energy-services center while creating industrial employment.
For NATO: Additional repair and maintenance capacity in the Eastern Mediterranean could improve operational resilience, subject to actual contracts and military requirements.
For China: The strategic relevance is particularly evident because U.S. congressional testimony has described the Elefsina financing as supporting American security objectives while countering Chinese acquisition interests. This should not be confused with evidence of an inevitable confrontation with Chinese-owned port operations. 
6. Implementation risks and opportunities: THE TRIDENT PLAN
U.S. Embassy – Elefsina Shipyards – Greece–U.S. Strategic Partnership
Strategic and geopolitical analysis | 19 October 2026
Executive assessment
The Trident Plan can be understood as a proposed strategic framework connecting American diplomatic influence, Greek shipbuilding capacity and the geopolitical importance of the Eastern Mediterranean.
Its central proposition is that Elefsina Shipyards could evolve from a revitalized industrial facility into a regional hub for maritime security, commercial shipbuilding, logistics and energy infrastructure, supported by Greek–American investment and cooperation.
The framework rests on three pillars:
Security: Naval maintenance, defense-industrial cooperation and protection of critical maritime infrastructure.
Economic development: Investment, skilled employment, technology transfer and shipbuilding competitiveness.
Energy transition: LNG-related maritime infrastructure, alternative-fuel vessels and cleaner industrial operations.
An important distinction: the infographic presents a strategic concept, not proof that the U.S. Embassy and Greek government have formally adopted every element as a single program called the Trident Plan.
1. Why Elefsina matters
Elefsina occupies a strategically valuable position near Athens, Piraeus and Salamis, combining industrial facilities with access to important Mediterranean shipping routes.
Its potential extends beyond ship repair. A competitive Elefsina industrial cluster could serve commercial shipping, naval vessels, energy-related maritime operations and regional logistics.
The significance for the United States lies in developing reliable industrial capacity in a NATO ally, reducing dependence on distant maintenance facilities and strengthening resilient supply chains.
For Greece, the opportunity is to transform foreign investment into lasting domestic productive capacity rather than merely increasing imports of foreign defense equipment.

At least one senior U.S. senator, government intelligence officials and the U.S. Army’s Office for Operations, Plans and Force Development are interested in reviewing the Russian capabilities, U.S. sources said.

In addition, International Healthline Corp. is planning to bring a team of Russian specialists here within the next couple of months to demonstrate the capability, company President Jim Hovis said in a Dec. 2 interview.

Meanwhile, the U.S. Army’s Armament Research, Development & Engineering Center is conducting a one-year study of acoustic beam technology that may mirror some of the effects reported by the Russians.

Army spokesman Bill Harris said Dec. 3 the command awarded the one-year study contract to Scientific Applications & Research Associates of Huntington Beach, Calif. Related research is being conducted at the Moscow-based Andreev Institute, U.S. and Russian sources said.

Despite the growing interest in a capability traditionally reserved for science fiction novels and cinema, industry and academic experts are cautious and skeptical about its potential battlefield use.

“This is not something that strikes me as requiring high-level attention,” Raymond Garthoff, a defense and intelligence analyst at the Washington-based Brookings Institution, said in a Dec. 2 interview.

Morris contends that the capability has been demonstrated in the laboratory in Russia and should be placed under international restrictions at the earliest possible opportunity.

text:
Any political candidate who does not want to call out or deal with Rhode Island’s problems-- problems that were created here in Rhode Island-- is not a serious candidate. Anyone whose messaging centers around national and DC rhetoric instead of the home fires does not deserve your vote.

My focus is on what’s going on right here-- which is why my personal votes will go to the people willing to deal with what’s going on right here. This doesn’t have to be party-partisan. This has to be centered on who’s best for a local job.

Some of the biggest names in the races are more concerned with blaming Washington than blaming the problems that started in Providence. Washington is not responsible for our RI economy, our healthcare crisis, our loss of jobs, the struggles in our education system, the difficulties faced by seniors, our failing infrastructure, or the fact that our state agencies are unable to deliver results. We need to worry about US.

Finger pointing signals a lack of honesty, accountability, and willingness to actually do the job.

If you choose your local candidates based upon national issues, that’s a problem. We need to focus on Rhode Island… and we need honest, decent people willing to do that work. Pay attention to what they tell you, and then believe them. If they say DC is the problem, you can bet your bottom dollar that they are not the solution.

Pay attention to the deep pockets, the campaign ads, and the overall messaging they send. Infighting and attacks are about personal power. They’re never about the people. Is the candidate telling you what they hope to do for you, or are they just telling you why some other guy is bad?

If a candidate has a 30-second ad and all they do is point out their opponent’s flaws, without telling you their own strengths, that probably means they don’t actually have any strengths.

I ran CLEAN campaigns focused on RI because I truly believe that’s the representation I wanted all my life-- and that was the representation I was going to bring. And I’ve lived up to that promise. I don’t win every fight, but I keep showing up with the voice of my constituents.

We need more regular everyday people who are willing to step into the arena and do the hard work. We don’t need more polished finger-pointers. That kind of campaign messaging offers us no solutions, just the same old, same old.

If you want more of the same, go ahead and vote for the people who aren’t willing to grapple with the reality of RI problems, but have tons of cash to blame others. 

BUT, If you truly want change, look for the people who talk about Rhode Island like it matters-- and who tell you what they will do, not just who they will blame.

And remember: endorsements are powerful. An endorsed candidate has allegiances. Many times those allegiances are in the best interest of the people, especially when they’re local. But there are a lot of endorsements out there that are only for the benefit of special interests. Follow the money. Ask whether those allegiances serve us in Rhode Island, or somewhere else.

This is my best advice, folks. You get ONE vote-- spend it like it's your last chip and you're about to lose the house.

RURAL IRELAND DESERVES BETTER. Over the weekend, I returned to Boyle, a town I called home for many years, to host a conference. Afterwards, I walked around and was saddened to see so many closed shops, boarded-up windows and empty premises.

Boyle is a beautiful town, but its high street is being hollowed out. Where is the Government’s plan to save our small businesses before it’s too late?

The draconian COVID measures devastated many small businesses. Six years later, those that survived are still struggling. Yet where is the meaningful support?

I understand there are plans for an Aldi in Boyle. It may create some jobs, but what about the independent businesses already fighting to survive? Across the country, small traders are struggling to compete hi with big chains and online giants like Amazon.

Think local. Shop local. Support local. Because if we don’t, these businesses simply won’t survive.

Do we really want our beautiful Irish towns to become rows of empty units, bookies, vape shops and mobile phone repair shops, losing the character that makes them special?

I spoke to a woman visiting from Australia who couldn’t find a steak for dinner in Boyle. Plenty of choice for Indian and Chinese cuisine- but nowhere serving traditional Irish fare. What does that say about the state of our town and the experience we offer visitors?

Our towns deserve better. Our small businesses deserve better. The Government must act before it’s too late.

#Boyle #ShopLocal #SupportSmallBusiness #SaveOurTowns

text:
🏇 CHELTENHAM WATCH | MONDAY 19 OCTOBER 2026

FROM THE CHAMPION BUMPER TO THE SUPREME? 

BASS HUNTER FACES HIS FIRST REAL JUMPING EXAMINATION

One of the most interesting horses on today's National Hunt programme is not an unknown prospect. He is a horse we have already seen perform with considerable credit at the Cheltenham Festival.

Chris Gordon's Bass Hunter makes his hurdling debut at Plumpton, seven months after finishing third in the Champion Bumper behind The Mourne Rambler and Mets Ta Ceinture.

That Cheltenham performance was particularly encouraging because Bass Hunter helped force the pace rather than benefiting from a patiently ridden race. He led for much of the contest and was still battling inside the final furlong, losing second place by just a short head.

He had previously won bumpers at Newbury and Ascot, including Listed company, and Gordon has never concealed the regard in which he holds the gelding.

The question now is whether that natural pace and enthusiasm can be channelled into an efficient round of hurdling. A horse who likes to attack his races must learn to conserve energy between obstacles if he is to progress towards the Supreme Novices' Hurdle.

Today's opposition provides a useful starting point.

🇫🇷 12:27 COMPIÈGNE | CYRIELLE
The €55,000 Prix de Saint-Raphaël brings together an intriguing collection of three-year-olds beginning their jumping careers.

Cyrielle makes her hurdling debut for Marcel Rolland, while The Mighty Murt represents the George and Zetterholm partnership. François Nicolle's Non Conformiste is another newcomer worth monitoring.

These are the sorts of French races where future British and Irish jumping prospects can first emerge. The important evidence will be how the newcomers travel, jump and finish, rather than simply which one wins.

🇬🇧 14:00 PLUMPTON | BASS HUNTER
This is the day's principal Cheltenham assignment.
Bass Hunter faces Anniversary, who won on his hurdling debut at Fontwell earlier this month and must concede weight for that success. Anniversary has already demonstrated that he can jump and win over obstacles. Bass Hunter brings the stronger bumper form, but must now prove he can reproduce that ability over hurdles.

Freddie Gordon knows him well, having ridden him prominently in the Champion Bumper. His ability to settle the horse and establish a comfortable jumping rhythm could be just as important as the finishing position. A fluent performance would strengthen Bass Hunter's credentials as a serious novice-hurdle prospect. A victory achieved through raw ability despite jumping mistakes would leave more questions unanswered.

🇫🇷 15:00 COMPIÈGNE | BANCASTER
The Prix Jumna offers another worthwhile examination of developing French hurdlers.

Bancaster returns for Mickaël Seror after a promising previous hurdles effort. Elle A Tout Ca, Provokateur and Magic Pal are among the opposition in this €49,000 contest for four-year-olds.

Today the dioceses of the United States celebrate the Memorial of St. Isaac Jogues and his companions. They were Jesuit missionaries who died as martyrs in North America where they preached the Gospel. They died between the years 1642-1649.

French Jesuits were the first missionaries to go to Canada and North America after J. Cartier discovered Canada in 1534. Their mission region extended from Nova Scotia to Maryland. Isaac Jogues, John de Brébeuf, Gabriel Lalemant, Noel Chabanel, Charles Garnier, Anthony Daniel, René Goupil and John de Lalande (the first six Jesuits, the last two laymen) preached the gospel to the Iroquois and Huron Indians, and after being tortured, they were martyred in the area of what is now Auriesville, New York. The martyrdoms took place between 1642 and 1649. Ten years after the martyrdom of St. Isaac Jogues, Kateri Tekakwitha was born in the same village in which he died. These martyrs are co-patrons of Canada.

The missionaries arrived in Canada less than a century after its discovery by Cartier in 1534, in the hope of converting the Indians and setting up "New France." Their opponents were often the English and Dutch colonists. When Isaac Jogues returned to Paris after his first capture and torture, he said to his superior: "Yes, Father, I want whatever our Lord wants, even if it costs a thousand lives." He had written in his mission report: "These tortures are very great, but God is still greater, and immense."

In the Office of Readings we have an excerpt from the mission journal of St. John de Brébeuf, who had been a student of the great Jesuit spiritual writer, Louis Lallemant. He wrote:

“For two days now I have experienced a great desire to be a martyr and to endure all the torments the martyrs suffered.... I vow to you, Jesus my Savior, that as far as I have the strength I will never fail to accept the grace of martyrdom, if some day you in your infinite mercy should offer it to me, your most unworthy servant.... On receiving the blow of death, I shall accept it from your hands with the fullest delight and joy of spirit.... My God, it grieves me greatly that you are not known, that in this savage wilderness all have not been converted to you, that sin has not been driven from it.” (Excerpted from Saints of the Roman Calendar by Enzo Lodi)

Dr. Jumana Nargawala and Dr. Fakhruddin Attar were accused of working together to mutilate the genitals of young girls in Michigan. Dr. Nargwala was the one who actually performed the procedures, while Dr. Attar provided her the space in which to operate.

The procedure Dr. Nargwala was accused of performing upon nine little girls involved the amputation of the clitoris and inner labia, followed by the removal of the flesh along the inside of the outer labia. Dr. Nargwala then allegedly sewed these little girls shut, leaving a hole the size of a matchstick for urination and menstruation. The indictment accused Dr. Attar of opening his clinic after hours so that Dr. Nargwala could mutilate the victims, and both physicians were accused of telling victims and their families not to discuss the mutilations. 

The case against both doctors was dismissed in 2018 after the judge ruled that the federal FGM statute was “unconstitutional.” Neither physician was ever charged in state courts, and Michigan’s Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs chose not to pursue disciplinary action. text:
OpenAI Teams with Hollywood for Sora Video AI Revival

As we start another week, today’s news brings an intriguing twist to the world of AI video technology. OpenAI is reportedly in talks with a new startup led by some big names from Hollywood to revive the shuttered Sora platform. But why now? And what does this mean for the future of AI in film production?

So, you’re asking: Is this just another tech buzz or something truly groundbreaking? What’s so special about Sora that it’s worth reviving? And how will this impact the broader landscape of AI tools used by filmmakers and content creators?

Let's dive into the details.
The Fall of Sora

In April 2026, OpenAI made a surprising move by shutting down both the app and web versions of Sora. This was followed by the API shutdown in September, effectively putting an end to what many saw as a promising AI video platform. But why did it happen? Was there something wrong with Sora’s technology or just a shift in priorities?

The reasons behind Sora's closure were not entirely clear at the time. Some speculated that OpenAI was pivoting its focus towards other areas of AI research, while others believed that regulatory concerns and ethical considerations played a role. Regardless of the exact cause, the shutdown left many users and developers wondering about the future of AI video technology.
The Rise Again

Fast forward to October 2026, and we see a new startup led by Jeffrey Katzenberg, Bill Pibbles (formerly of OpenAI), and Sudhaj Jaswa stepping into the spotlight. This team aims to leverage deep access to Sora’s core model for professional video production software and services. In return, OpenAI would receive a stake in this venture.
The Players
• Jeffrey Katzenberg: A legendary figure in Hollywood known for founding DreamWorks Animation and leading Walt Disney Studios.
• Bill Pibbles: Former head of Sora research at OpenAI, bringing intimate knowledge of the platform’s architecture.
• Sudhaj Jaswa: Ex-Dropbox CFO with extensive experience in tech finance.
The Timeline
• April 17, 2026: Bill Pibbles announces his departure from OpenAI.
• April 26, 2026: Sora app and web version shut down.
• September 9, 2026: Katzenberg and Pibbles’ new startup is revealed; plans to train their own video models emerge.
• September 24, 2026: Sora API officially shuts down.
• October 12, 2026: Talks with OpenAI about accessing the core Sora model begin.
The Motivation

For Katzenberg and Pibbles, this move is driven by a desire to continue their work on cutting-edge AI video technology. They see an opportunity in Hollywood’s demand for advanced visual effects and content creation. For OpenAI, it's about financial gain from an innovative project that could push the boundaries of what AI can do.

But here’s where things get interesting: If this new startup decides to train its own models rather than just modifying Sora, we might see a new player emerge in the competitive landscape of AI video tools. This could shake up the industry and introduce fresh dynamics.
How It Works

Sora was designed as an end-to-end platform for generating high-quality videos using AI. The core model at the heart of Sora is capable of understanding complex visual data, creating realistic animations, and integrating various elements seamlessly into a cohesive video output. By leveraging this technology, Katzenberg’s team aims to create specialized tools that cater specifically to professional filmmakers.

The process involves training new models based on existing Sora architecture but tailored for specific use cases in film production. This could include everything from generating concept art to automating the creation of visual effects and even assisting with storyboarding and editing processes.
What Is Stored

When users interacted with Sora, they would upload various types of data such as video clips, images, text descriptions, and audio files. The platform used this data to train its models and generate new content. However, once the shutdown occurred, all user-generated data was deleted in accordance with OpenAI’s privacy policies.
What Is Excluded

It's important to note that Sora never stored personal information beyond what was necessary for account management purposes. This included basic contact details like email addresses but excluded any sensitive or personally identifiable information (PII). Additionally, the platform did not retain any data related to user interactions after a certain period of inactivity.
User Controls

During its active phase, Sora provided users with several controls over their data and privacy settings. Users could manage their account details, delete uploaded content, and opt out of receiving promotional emails or notifications from OpenAI. These features ensured that users had control over how their information was used within the platform.
Availability

As of now, there is no official word on when or if Sora will be available again under its new guise. The startup led by Katzenberg and Pibbles is still in the early stages of development, with plans to secure additional funding before launching any products. Until then, interested parties can follow updates through OpenAI’s official channels.
What This Does Not Prove

It's crucial to remember that while this partnership between Hollywood and AI experts looks promising on paper, it does not automatically guarantee success or innovation in the field of film production. The challenges ahead include navigating regulatory landscapes, addressing ethical concerns, and ensuring that the technology meets the high standards expected by professional filmmakers.
Practical Takeaway

For those interested in the intersection of AI and film production, this development offers a glimpse into how established industries might embrace cutting-edge technologies to enhance their workflows. Whether you’re a filmmaker looking for new tools or an AI enthusiast curious about real-world applications, keeping an eye on Katzenberg’s venture could provide valuable insights.

So, what do you think? Is this a step forward or just another twist in the ever-evolving world of AI video technology?

Discuss your thoughts in the comments below!

text:
A branding consultant wants to reposition toward tech and AI companies. For a B2B AI founder thinking about their own positioning, this is how I'd approach that work.

(1) Choose the situation he wants to be hired for.

Branding for AI companies leaves a lot open. A founder explaining a new product category needs different help from a company whose buyers keep confusing it with cheaper alternatives. I'd investigate which situation fits his experience.

(2) Understand why past customers sought help.

What had become difficult? Why did they hire him then? Which problems does he want to solve again? Those answers would help us narrow the buyer beyond a company size or industry label.

(3) Find the expertise he can demonstrate.

I'd ask him to walk me through past branding decisions: what he changed, why he chose it and what evidence supports the outcome. Explaining that reasoning gives a buyer a way to assess his judgment.

(4) Establish where his AI knowledge applies.

Which products and buyer problems does he understand well enough to discuss? Where does he need more research or hands-on experience? We'd build around the expertise he can support and keep learning where the gaps are.

(5) Define what a buyer can hire him to do.

What problem would the engagement address? What would the buyer receive? What input would he need from them? These answers give the offer boundaries and keep the promise tied to work he can deliver.

(6) Write the copy around the buyer's situation.

Suppose the research points to founders whose buyers struggle to understand the product's value. We'd test language describing that problem and support it with relevant work. The buyer gets something more specific to evaluate than AI branding expert..

(7) Turn his reasoning into content.

He could explain how he'd investigate a confusing homepage, what he'd ask before recommending a new brand direction and why a message fits a particular buyer. Public breakdowns would be labelled as his analysis. Client examples would need evidence and permission.

Each post would let a potential buyer inspect part of his thinking before a call.

This is how I'd connect the research, offer and writing. The buyer we choose determines which proof matters. That proof limits what we can promise. The offer gives the content something specific to explain.

text:
Read those following books: 
Mike Moore's Twilight War: The Folly of U.S. Space Dominance—a critical, historical analysis examining the geopolitics, military strategy, and security risks of space weaponization and unilateral dominance.

Astropolitik: Classical Geopolitics in the Space Age by Everett C. Dolman
Written by an Air Force strategist quoted in Twilight War, this book provides the counterpoint doctrine that Moore critiques. 
Dolman applies classical realpolitik to orbital space, arguing how and why a nation might seek space dominance. 
Reading it alongside Twilight War provides a comprehensive view of both sides of the space-control debate.

Space as a Strategic Asset by Joan Johnson-Freese
Examines the dual-use nature of satellite technology and how aggressive U.S. posture in space risks triggering counter-measures from China and Russia. 
Like Moore, Johnson-Freese advocates for multilateral international cooperation and diplomacy over unilateral military dominance.

War in Space: Strategy, Spacepower, Geopolitics by Bleddyn E. Bowen
Offers a modern theoretical framework for space warfare, arguing that spacepower is inherently linked to terrestrial military operations and politics. 
It builds on the strategic ideas Moore covers, focusing on the practical and political limits of weaponizing orbit.

Broader Military Strategy, Arms Control & Technology Policy The Tragedy of Great Power Politics by John J. Mearsheimer The Connection: 

Mearsheimer praised Twilight War for its clear-eyed political realistic grounding. 
This foundational work on offensive realism explains the systemic international pressures that drive major powers to seek total dominance—the exact strategic impulse Moore argues is counterproductive in space.

The Wizards of Armageddon by Fred Kaplan
A classic history of the nuclear strategists and intellectuals who developed Cold War deterrence doctrines. 
If you found Moore’s historical deep-dive into early space strategists and nuclear-era policies compelling, Kaplan's work uncovers the same institutional mindsets regarding nuclear warfighting and technological superiority. 

Kill Chain: The Rise of the High-Tech Autocrats by Andrew Cockburn
Critiques the U.S. military-industrial complex's obsession with technological "silver bullets," precision targeting, and overhead surveillance. 
It aligns with Moore’s argument regarding the hubris of relying strictly on high-tech military dominance.

Astropolitik: Classical Geopolitics in the Space Age by Everett C. Dolman
Written by an Air Force strategist quoted in Twilight War, this book provides the counterpoint doctrine that Moore critiques.
Dolman applies classical realpolitik to orbital space, arguing how and why a nation might seek space dominance.
Reading it alongside Twilight War provides a comprehensive view of both sides of the space-control debate.

Space as a Strategic Asset by Joan Johnson-Freese
Examines the dual-use nature of satellite technology and how aggressive U.S. posture in space risks triggering counter-measures from China and Russia.
Like Moore, Johnson-Freese advocates for multilateral international cooperation and diplomacy over unilateral military dominance.

War in Space: Strategy, Spacepower, Geopolitics by Bleddyn E. Bowen
Offers a modern theoretical framework for space warfare, arguing that spacepower is inherently linked to terrestrial military operations and politics.
It builds on the strategic ideas Moore covers, focusing on the practical and political limits of weaponizing orbit.

Broader Military Strategy, Arms Control & Technology Policy The Tragedy of Great Power Politics by John J. Mearsheimer The Connection:

Mearsheimer praised Twilight War for its clear-eyed political realistic grounding.
This foundational work on offensive realism explains the systemic international pressures that drive major powers to seek total dominance—the exact strategic impulse Moore argues is counterproductive in space.

The Wizards of Armageddon by Fred Kaplan
A classic history of the nuclear strategists and intellectuals who developed Cold War deterrence doctrines.
If you found Moore’s historical deep-dive into early space strategists and nuclear-era policies compelling, Kaplan's work uncovers the same institutional mindsets regarding nuclear warfighting and technological superiority.

Kill Chain: The Rise of the High-Tech Autocrats by Andrew Cockburn
Critiques the U.S. military-industrial complex's obsession with technological "silver bullets," precision targeting, and overhead surveillance.
It aligns with Moore’s argument regarding the hubris of relying strictly on high-tech military dominance.

text:
A bullhorn acacia and an anchor tenant expose why a government would lend money to a multibillionaire investor

Look closely at the hollow swelling near the base of these thorns, Sarah said, tapping the branch of the bullhorn acacia tree. It spends a substantial fraction of its daily metabolic energy manufacturing sugar nectar and growing hollow homes. It doesn't consume those sugars itself. It gives them away to a colony of aggressive ants that do nothing to pollinate its flowers.

It looks like blatant waste, James replied, watching tiny ants swarm across the leaves. A tree giving free food and housing to an entity that is already capable of surviving on its own sounds like a bad allocation of resources.

That is because you're looking at the tree and the ant as two separate individuals trading food for work, Sarah said. The ant doesn't just eat the nectar. It patrols every square centimetre of the surrounding ground. It stings any herbivore that touches a leaf, and it clips down every single climbing vine that tries to grow within a two metre radius.

The tree isn't paying for labour. It is paying to clear a space in an overcrowded forest where smaller plants can't survive.

So the subsidy isn't about feeding the ant, James said. The subsidy creates a zone of structural safety around the tree that alters the behaviour of everything nearby.

Exactly, Sarah said. Now think about why a state government would offer $200 million in cheap loans and tax relief to a multibillionaire building a new cargo airport, while charging full taxes on every small local shop in town.

The common explanation is political corruption or corporate welfare, James said. People assume a billionaire has enough private wealth to fund their own project, so lending them public money at 2% interest seems absurd.

And that assumption fails because it misunderstands what the state is actually buying, Sarah said. A multibillionaire doesn't need the cheap loan to afford the concrete. The cheap loan exists to force the investor to act as an anchor tenant for regional risk.

Explain how an anchor tenant operates in commercial real estate, James said.

In a shopping mall, the owner gives the massive department store thousands of square metres of space almost rent free, Sarah said. Meanwhile, the small coffee shop, the boutique clothing store, and the dry cleaner pay high rent per square metre. If you look at rent per square metre, it looks like a giveaway to a rich corporation.

But without the department store committing to open its doors, ten thousand shoppers won't walk through the building every week. The coffee shop won't sign a lease, the bank won't extend a business loan to the boutique, and the logistics company won't build a delivery route.

So the anchor tenant solves a coordination problem, James said. Smaller businesses can't take the risk of moving in first because they don't have the scale to guarantee foot traffic.

Precisely, Sarah said. The anchor tenant absorbs the initial coordination risk. The government loan to a multibillionaire works the exact same way.

When the state provides a cheap 30 year loan for a $2 billion industrial hub, it isn't enriching the billionaire. It is buying a public signal. The loan contract obligates the investor to deploy massive private capital in a specific location. Once that anchor is locked into place, three hundred specialised machine suppliers, two regional transport lines, five technical colleges, and 1,000 housing developers suddenly know the market will exist.

They don't need to coordinate with each other, James said. They only need to coordinate with the anchor.

That is the core mechanism, Sarah said. The government uses concessional finance to lower the anchor hurdle rate just enough to force a massive private commitment. The secondary network of smaller firms then moves in, paying full taxes and creating thousands of jobs. The state recovers its loan concession many times over through the surrounding tax base that wouldn't exist without the cleared space.

Where does this explanation stop working? James asked. Because governments clearly throw money at wealthy investors for projects that fail completely.

It breaks down when the anchor takes the nectar without defending the tree, Sarah said. In nature, certain parasitic ant species move into the bullhorn acacia thorns, consume the nectar, and run away when a caterpillar arrives.

In an economy, if the billionaire uses the cheap loan to build something that doesn't generate dense secondary investment, or if the government subsidises an investor who would have built the project anyway, the public money becomes pure rent extraction.

So the loan is only justified if it changes the anchor decision, and if the anchor presence forces a network of uncoordinated secondary investments to appear, James said.

That is the test, Sarah said. The state isn't lending money to wealth. It is paying for a structural centre of gravity.

Beijing’s decision to elevate Huawei into the standard-bearer of Chinese technological self-reliance has turned the telecom giant into an unintended proxy for public criticism of the Party-state.

The latest controversy erupted on October 8 when Chinese automotive platform Dongchedi released a test video showing the brake pedal brackets of three new Maextro V800 luxury minivans—a flagship vehicle launched by Huawei and built by JAC Motors—snapping during repeated emergency stops from 100 kilometers per hour.

Despite official marketing advertising the vehicle's braking systems as having "multiple redundancies, as stable as Mount Tai," the revelation sent JAC shares tumbling to their daily loss limits on consecutive days.

The issue escalated into a political flashpoint as censors intervened overnight, removing the review video across major platforms including Bilibili, Douyin, and Weibo under vague violation notices.

Online commentary swiftly shifted from automotive safety to state censorship, with internet users sarcastically observing that Huawei had achieved "strong leadership over the theoretical mouthpieces and the public opinion front" on the Party’s behalf.

Because open dissent against the Chinese Communist Party carries severe legal consequences, expressing grievances through product complaints against a state-backed corporate icon offers a comparatively safer outlet for public discontent over censorship, corporate impunity, and state favoritism.

Huawei’s untouchable status took root after 2019 U.S. export controls turned its products into vehicles of patriotic consumption, an aura reinforced by state propaganda during the detention and release of CFO Meng Wanzhou, as well as an estimated $30 billion in state backing.

The resultant climate bound Huawei so closely to Chinese national pride that questioning its engineering or marketing was routinely cast by defenders and censors as an attack on domestic industry.

Public pushback has manifested in three distinct tiers, beginning with biting parody of the company's bombastic marketing language, such as comparing executive Yu Chengdong’s voice and slogans to a vibrating children's bamboo cicada toy.

Huawei’s legal efforts to suppress those viral videos under corporate defamation rules triggered a classic Streisand effect, prompting social media users to flood platforms with veiled puns and references to past political speech crackdowns.

A second tier of criticism targets Huawei's treatment of ordinary citizens, most notably the 2018 case of former employee Li Hongyuan, who spent 251 days in detention following a company report before being cleared, which spawned the subversive numerical meme "985, 996, 251, 404" attacking grueling work cultures and online censorship.

The third tier links the conglomerate directly to top leadership, with online satirists openly acknowledging that venting frustration against Huawei acts as a stand-in for anger directed at Beijing's political elite.

Cracks in state support have begun to emerge, with provincial propaganda organs in Zhejiang and Jiangsu publicly urging the company to welcome scrutiny and cautioning against an "irrational mentality of shielding one's own."

The brake failure incident underscores this shifting dynamic, as central state media notably declined to shield Huawei, and the People’s Daily published a pointed commentary declaring that a car's brake pedal should never break under normal driving conditions.

While Beijing will continue relying on Huawei as a cornerstone of its technological ambitions, the erosion of public deference suggests the central leadership may quietly put distance between state propaganda and the company’s corporate missteps.

What, then, does it mean to tell the Ukrainians: "Hold on for just one more winter"?

Pushing people into freezing cold, darkness, hunger, and the total collapse of the state—under the pretense that they can "somehow hold out until spring"—is to condemn the Ukrainian population to a humanitarian catastrophe of biblical proportions. 

If a 90-billion loan or a European defense fund were truly intended to serve the people, they would look quite different. Instead, these funds act as oxygen for a machine that relies on maintaining a state of emergency; the moment the guns fall silent, the entire system—built on subsidies, political lies, and control over the population—would collapse.

Zelenskyy embraces European leaders, who offer him symbolic pats on the back—yet with the U.S. stepping away from the table and Trump having dismantled sanctions, this entire European structure is now condemned to witness its own geopolitical failure.

What is unfolding in Ukraine is not "aid" to an attacked nation in the traditional sense. It is a managed economic and demographic collapse, in which the country is being systematically drained to the very marrow. The financial injections Kyiv is currently demanding are not intended for development; rather, they serve to keep the patient on life support, allowing corporations and creditors to finish buying up whatever remains.

It is a deranged, cold, and inhumane calculation—a calculation that serves as a grim reminder that words have always preceded the bullets. Before the first blow is struck, someone must—over a long period, systematically, and at a staggering financial cost—prepare the ground within people’s minds. They must dehumanize the other side, foster a binary worldview—"good versus evil," "us versus them"—and destroy nuanced thinking, replacing it with dogmas and icons. They must clog the capacity of the human mind with a crude, aggressive propaganda of universal hatred—a hatred directed at everyone, woven into a politics that thrives on exploitation. Behind this stand those who lay claim to the fruits of the labor of the very people they dehumanize. These targets might be neighbors, colleagues, voters of opposing political factions, or even entire nations.

Propaganda acts as an invisible architect, constructing corridors for violence. Unless we begin to scrutinize, weigh, and reject the words that manufacture war, we will be left doing nothing but endlessly counting amputations, orphans, and widows.

text:
Tyler Perry is worth $1.4 billion and he fired his own aunt for not showing up to work.

When his mom died, he mailed the rest of the family letters. 60 days to get a job, or the money stops.

Now here's the thing. Back in the early '90s, that same guy was sleeping in his car.

He's 6'5" and the car was a Geo Metro, so picture that for a minute.

In 1992 he took every dollar he had, about $12,000 from selling used cars plus a tax refund, and put on his first play in Atlanta. He figured 1,200 people would show up that weekend. Thirty did. His rent and his car payment were riding on that show, so when it flopped, he lost the apartment too.

And he kept going. He put the play up again the next year, and the year after that, and lost money every single time until the seventh try finally sold out in 1998.

Seven years later Diary of a Mad Black Woman opened at #1 and made $22 million its first weekend. He kept ownership of what he made, and eventually turned 330 acres of an old Army base in Atlanta into his own studio. Forbes has him at $1.4 billion now.

His mom, Maxine, was the reason he kept pushing through all of it. He's said as much. She asked him to look after the family, so he did, for years, the whole time she was alive. She passed in December 2009, and that's when the letters went out.

If you've lived what he lived, you know which part actually made you. It was six years of failing with nobody coming to save him. A monthly check from a rich relative takes exactly that away from somebody.

So with his aunt, he tried a job first. She'd call asking for money, he'd send it, and finally he offered her a spot so she could build something with him. She kept calling in and not showing up, so she was out.

According to Perry, every relative who got that letter found a job. Some of those jobs didn't pay much, and he said he didn't care, he wanted them proud of a paycheck they earned themselves.

He told Derrick Hayes, the guy who started Big Dave's Cheesesteaks, to watch out for family "putting holes in the boat" while you're trying to get across. Sometimes, he said, you build the boat by yourself and have everybody wait on the shore.

He runs the same rules with his son Aman, who does chores to get paid.

Honestly, he gave them the best thing he had. Sixty days and nobody coming to save them, which is the exact deal he got in 1992, and it's the deal that made him a billionaire.

Never before in history has a party adopted a war strategy to maximize civilian deaths on its own side. On October 13, Israeli military commanders told Palestinians living in Gaza to evacuate to the south. The northern half of the strip is full of Hamas assets—from rockets to rifles, communications gear to personnel—that Israel plans to destroy in the coming days of the war. But Hamas leaders demanded that the people stay in place. Why? While some of Hamas’s most brutal tactics, like systematic rape and beheading captives, are long-practiced atrocities for which the armies of Stalin, Hitler, and Genghis Khan are infamous, it is unprecedented for a party to adopt a war strategy to maximize civilian deaths on its own side. This is so strange and evil that it should appall any decent person. Contrary to conventional commentary, this is not a human shield strategy. It’s a human sacrifice strategy. Since its birth in 1987, Hamas has declared its aim to destroy Israel. Its strategy is asymmetric—that is, because Hamas is smaller and weaker than the Israeli Army, it relies on a strategy designed to undermine Israel politically. In hopes (presumably) that it can induce Saudi leaders to drop their plans to normalize relations with Israel, Hamas launched this war with two goals. First, to provoke uprisings among Arabs and Muslims, both within and outside Israel. Second, to cause the rest of the world to view Israel with disgust and hatred. To achieve these aims, Hamas is ensuring that its war will harm and kill large numbers of Palestinians in Gaza. To bring this about, it has strategized and laid groundwork for years. Its aim is to propagandize a gullible world—to put the blood of Palestinian victims on Israel’s hands. Defense officials in numerous countries, for operational reasons and to comply with international laws of war, take pains to locate their military assets away from their civilians and to maximize protection for the latter. Hamas officials do the opposite. As United Nations officials and others have disapprovingly noted, Hamas stores ammunition in schools, puts missile launchers adjacent to mosques, sets up command centers in hospitals, and generally bases its operations in densely populated civilian neighborhoods. This is not simply a human-shield strategy, where the aim is to deter an attack by using innocent lives as a barrier. Hamas is doing something far more insidious: it’s ensuring the mass death of Palestinians. Here is Hamas official Ali Baraka summing up the difference between the two worldviews: “The Israelis are known to love life. We, on the other hand, sacrifice ourselves. We consider our dead to be martyrs.” When Hamas fires rockets at Israel and kills, captures, and rapes civilians there, they know Israel will retaliate. Hamas leaders put their assets in civilian buildings not in hopes that Israel will hold fire, but in a cold calculation that the retaliation will do terrible harm to Palestinian civilians—despite the extraordinary efforts Israel’s army makes to avoid it. Hamas is working to maximize, not minimize, that harm. This is to generate international pressure on Israel to end its retaliation—and to strengthen Israel’s enemies in their depiction of the Jewish state as a villain. Israel has moral and practical reasons for avoiding harm to Palestinian civilians. Israelis pride themselves on acting humanely, even in war. Their military officers—like those in the U.S. military—distinguish between civilian and military sites and never purposefully target the former. Even when attacking senior terrorist leaders, Israel tries to avoid harming their family members, let alone unrelated civilians. To avert collateral damage, Israel routinely provides warnings of attacks, even though they increase risk to Israelis and decrease an attack’s chances of success. In the current war, Israel has notified Gazans in various neighborhoods that there would soon be attacks there and they should hasten to designated safe areas. Hamas’s strategy is innovative in the worst way. For everyone who aspires to strengthen moral constraints on warfare, it is a huge step backward. It is savage, cynical, and unnatural—but what’s worse, it’s effective. That is why it’s being used. Innocent Palestinians deserve sympathy. But when Americans, Europeans, and others misdirect their outrage at Israel, failing to grasp Hamas’s responsibility, they are encouraging the very cruelty they intend to condemn. Blame for the purposeful sacrificing of innocent Palestinians goes first and foremost to Hamas, to be sure, but also to those of us in the outside world duped by this strategy. Schools, hospitals, and mosques will be bombed in the coming days. This is what Hamas wants, what it has made sure will happen. Those, however well-intentioned, who blame Israel are complicit in Hamas’s war crimes. It’s time to place the blame rightly and stop incentivizing Hamas’s crimes against the Palestinians (let alone against the Israelis). For the sake of both Palestinians and Israelis, and to honor basic decency and law, it is the least we can do.

Douglas J. Feith (2023)

https://t.co/YVoVgEHVB9 filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in mid-October 2026. Disney, whose former https://t.co/YVoVgEHVB9 chief executive Karandeep Anand became Disney's first chief technology officer on October 2, 2026, has submitted a stalking horse bid of $20m for a non-exclusive, perpetual licence to https://t.co/YVoVgEHVB9's training, safety, and serving system code plus 9 patents. A binding term sheet filed in the US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware on October 13 reveals that Disney has agreed to make employment offers to at least 60 https://t.co/YVoVgEHVB9 employees, the majority of the workforce, at an estimated annual compensation run rate of $60m; a $30m retention pool payable over 2 years brings the estimated 3-year total to approximately $180m. The vast majority of those offered positions accepted.

The licence explicitly excludes the https://t.co/YVoVgEHVB9 app, brand, domain names, user data, chat logs, training data, and finished models, which remain in the bankruptcy estate for other bidders. A $5.5m non-refundable up-front payment is included in the term sheet. Rival bids must exceed $21.7m (the $20m offer plus a $700,000 break-up fee and a $1m increment), be in cash, and close by November 30, 2026; an auction is scheduled for November 23 if competing bids emerge.

Disney is spending approximately 9 times more on the people than on the technology licence. The appointment of Mr Anand as Disney's first CTO before the bankruptcy filing, followed by the subsequent acqui-hire of the majority of his former team, suggests the transaction was structured in advance of the Chapter 11 filing. The https://t.co/YVoVgEHVB9 precedent follows Google's $2.7bn licensing deal with the company in August 2024, which brought its founders to Google; the same company's talent has now been absorbed by 2 of the world's largest technology and media businesses in succession.

THE GARDEN MAY BE DESTROYED, BUT SPRING CANNOT BE STOPPED! | RAJU PARULEKAR & PROF. RAVIKANT

In a powerful conversation, political commentator Raju Parulekar and Professor Ravikant discuss Rahul Gandhi's political journey, the legacies of Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, the dangers of majoritarian politics, and the enduring strength of democratic resistance.

THEIR MESSAGE DESERVES OUR ATTENTION:

A political script does not always reveal its hero at the beginning. Sometimes, defeat becomes a lesson, struggle builds credibility, and time changes how people understand a leader. Raju Parulekar offers his own interpretation of Rahul Gandhi's journey and India's changing political landscape.

But the discussion goes beyond individuals.

Gandhi and Ambedkar had different approaches, yet understanding their contributions together is essential to understanding India's struggle for freedom, social equality and constitutional justice. Their legacies should not become weapons for dividing people who are fighting against injustice.

The conversation also raises an uncomfortable question about caste, social privilege and the selective use of morality. Social equality cannot become a slogan while historical discrimination and present-day inequalities remain unexamined.

And then comes the most important message for every citizen engaged in democratic resistance:

OUR MORALITY IS OUR STRENGTH.

The struggle against authoritarian tendencies cannot succeed by abandoning the very values we seek to defend. Anger may awaken people, but justice, truth, compassion and non-violence can sustain a movement.

As the speakers suggest through the metaphor of a ruined garden, those in power may damage democratic institutions, but they cannot permanently control the aspirations of a determined people.

SPRING WILL COME — BUT DEMOCRACY MUST BE WATERED BY COURAGE, UNITY, CONSTITUTIONAL VALUES AND CONTINUOUS PUBLIC PARTICIPATION.

Do not surrender your conscience to political hatred. Read, question, debate, organise peacefully and stand with every citizen whose rights are threatened.

Our objective is not to replace one form of domination with another. It is to build an India where liberty, equality, fraternity and justice belong to everyone.

RESIST WITH COURAGE. STAND WITH CONSCIENCE. NEVER ABANDON HUMANITY.

Source: Ravi Kant Chandan (@profravikant) — conversation featuring Raju Parulekar.

I'm not answering from a 'Christian' point of view simply because I can't put myself in a Christian point of view..

The Bible is clear that the meaning of the covenant with the children of Israel was far more EARTH BASED than  spiritual. The main reason for the covenant God made with Israel was for the promised land (Canaan) and afterward expanded to preserving the atonement, an annual offering of the blood of a spotless lamb before God for the Passover,
The summary of  'this first covenant'  does not mean the only covenant, the topic in Hebrews is the blood covenant with the children of  Israel, through the Law of Moses.

The mention of the ritual blood sacrifices of bulls and goats is connected to the temporary cleansing from transgression, it had no lasting effect and after the final atonement has no meaning at all. The more permanent solution, the better solution was the blood of the spotless Lamb of God, the blood offer of Jesus Christ.

Even though Old Testament and New Testament may seems disconnected, it actually isn't disconnected at all.   The thinking of some is that it never changed, but the 'first' covenant with the children of Israel was not going to survive and the history of the children of Israel and the prophecies backs that up. 
This 'old' covenant was already hanging by threads, it was dissolving, beyond salvage and the promised land was already gone until only Judea remained during the time of the ministry of Jesus Christ. And God did  not do this, the children of Israel did this. 
And Jesus came to end it for good by replacing the dependence on law with the righteousness of God.

text:
ICYMI O/N & WEEKEND

MACRO:

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said AI-market turmoil would pass, arguing the industry remains early in a transformative investment cycle and returns justify continued spending. (BBG)

BofA says customer VIX-call positioning is approaching the heightened summer-2024 levels. Its model estimates a 10-point front-month VIX-futures jump could force dealer hedge buying equivalent to 90% of normal daily volume. (BBG)

At least 47 large US data centres projects have been delayed, withdrawn or blocked this year, according to RegLayer. Bernstein estimates only 35% of the planned pipeline is credible amid financing, power and local-opposition constraints. (FT)

SemiAnalysis forecasts over 50GW of new data-centre capacity in 2027, citing more than 24GW in advanced construction across 40 campuses. It sees memory and logic chips as the next potential bottleneck. (SemiAnalysis)

Shorecliff’s Grant Nachman said a large unsecured neocloud bond sale would now be prohibitively expensive or fail. Investors are demanding collateral, cash-flow visibility and stronger protections. (BBG)

Stress had spread beyond CoreWeave into investment-grade data-centre bonds by Friday’s close, WSJ reported. Analysts said local-running Apple and Meta models added to concerns about future data-centre demand. (WSJ)

Anthropic is pitching a safety bill allowing a judge to halt models posing specified imminent risks of over $1bn in damage or more than 50 deaths/serious injuries. The proposal requires testing and independent evaluations. (RTRS)

Barclays now expects Fed hikes in both December and January followed by a prolonged hold, versus its previous forecast for one final 25bp increase in December. (WSJ)

The AI selloff is pressuring crowded Treasury shorts, with systematic funds starting to cover. Julius Baer favours intermediate-duration bonds, arguing an AI-led demand shock could restore their equity-hedge role. (BBG)

Foreign Treasury holdings rose $83bn to $9.33tn in August. Japan’s fell $36bn and China’s fell $27bn to an 18-year low; UK holdings exceeded $1tn for the first time. Figures include valuation effects. (BBG)

Commercial-property buyers are renegotiating prices or shelving transactions as borrowing costs undermine valuations. Several investors are seeking single-digit discounts, with owners resisting crystallised losses. (FT)

An FT survey of 94 economists found 54% expect significant AI productivity gains across many or nearly all G20 countries over the next decade. Most expect changing jobs rather than mass unemployment. (FT)

Democrats led Republicans 52%–44% among likely voters on the generic congressional ballot in the October 9–13 ABC/Ipsos/Washington Post poll. Trump’s approval among adults was 33%, with 66% disapproving. (ABC News)

Holiday air fares are heading for their highest levels in at least a decade: Thanksgiving tickets average 31% above last year and Christmas 23% higher, Hopper says. Airlines report demand holding up. (WSJ)

BoJ’s Ueda said underlying inflation was very close to 2%, warning that long-term yields could rise if markets judged the pace of tightening inadequate. (BBG)

Japanese PM Takaichi rejected claims that her policies were driving yen weakness and higher yields, pledging fiscal discipline and control over bond issuance next fiscal year. (BBG)

China’s Q3 GDP grew 4.5% y/y versus 4.4% expected and 4.3% previously, taking year-to-date growth to 4.6% within Beijing’s 4.5–5% target. Quarterly growth was 1.2% versus 1.1% expected. (BBG, RTRS)

China’s September industrial production rose 5.5% y/y and retail sales increased 1.1%. January–September fixed-asset investment fell 7.2%, with property investment down 20.6%. (BBG)

China’s home prices fell at a slower pace in September, spurring hopes that the battered real estate market is turning a corner as the latest stimulus takes effect. (BBG)

China’s September coal output fell 6.8% y/y to 385m tonnes as winter-supply concerns build. Prices are at a three-year high, although the industry association sees limited risk of a nationwide shortage. (Bloomberg)

RBA’s Kent said the labour market was loosening faster than forecast and rates were somewhat restrictive, but whether they were restrictive enough remained uncertain. Next week’s inflation data will inform November’s decision. (BBG)

Alberta votes Monday on greater provincial powers and steps towards a binding separation referendum, not immediate independence. Separate polls put support for remaining in Canada at 66% for Angus Reid, 68% for Abacus and 70% for Leger. (FT, BBG, WSJ)

BoC’s Macklem said higher oil prices were boosting growth through exports, incomes and investment while also lifting inflation. He expects an upward inflation revision October 28; further hikes remain an open question. (BBG)

French 10-year OAT yields rose 6bp to 4.849% in Monday’s opening trade following the unrest in France, while Bund yields fell 0.7bp to 3.403%. (WSJ)

Nearly 2,400 people were arrested and around 1,000 police and firefighters injured in French cost-of-living unrest. Macron condemned the violence and promised dialogue, adding pressure ahead of the government’s budget battle. (FT)

Macron threatened tougher action, including possible protest bans, and demanded explanations for intelligence failures. Unions called another strike for November 5; Carrefour said about 20 stores were looted. (Bloomberg)

Macron rejected Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez’s resignation Monday morning and asked him to establish new measures against looters. (Sky News)

More than 160 people were arrested during a second night of looting around Milan’s Piazza del Duomo, Corriere reported. Meloni convened a public-order meeting. (Corriere reporting via Faytuks)

ECB officials leaned towards December for a third rate hike during the Bangkok meetings. (BBG)

ECB's Lagarde said the energy shock was too large for monetary policy simply to look through. She urged fiscal sustainability and said energy relief should be temporary and targeted. (BBG)

M&G, Ninety One and others are buying gilts ahead of the Budget, betting on fiscal credibility. UBS sees scope for roughly a 20bp fall in 10-year yields if it lands smoothly. (BBG)

Major UK retailers are cutting Christmas hiring: John Lewis plans 10,400 seasonal staff, down 3,300; Sainsbury’s is cutting 1,500 roles and Tesco 500 versus last year. (Bloomberg)

UK home asking prices rose 1% in October to £371,015, with London up 2.5%, Rightmove said. These are asking prices; 40% of London listings remain below their original advertised price. (BBG)

Hungary’s Magyar is due to unveil his 2027 Budget Monday, with investors seeking a credible path from a deficit above 7% towards 3% and eventual euro adoption. (BBG)

Indonesian stocks fell as much as 5.4% Monday after Friday’s rout following MSCI’s classification warning. Authorities cut the maximum daily share-price decline to 7% from 15% through year-end. (BBG)

Indonesian officials are due to meet MSCI online Monday afternoon to clarify the threat of standalone-market classification and the reforms needed to retain index access. (BBG)

Taiwan’s central bank pledged intervention when necessary after the currency reached its weakest since April 2025. ING and OCBC nevertheless see year-end recoveries to 31.50 and 31.60 per dollar. (BBG)

Vietnam’s prime minister set a 2027 growth target of at least 10%, with inflation around 4.5%, and called for lower lending rates to support production and exports. (BBG)

Vietnam plans to launch VN30 index options in Q1 2027, with testing in November and December. The product follows the FTSE upgrade and aims to attract foreign participation. (BBG)

The WMO expects El Niño to peak in December and persist until at least February 2027. Its Niño 3.4 forecast is 3.7°C above the long-term average—potentially a record—with implications for crops, electricity and shipping. (FT)

IRAN:

The US has recently almost completely stopped conducting strikes against Iranian anti-ship missiles and attack drone launchers in the strait. The pause was ordered by the White House to avoid escalating the war ahead of the midterm elections, but it has made Iran more confident about launching attacks, a U.S. official said. (Axios)

Trump endorsed Netanyahu ahead of Israel’s October 27 election and threatened to “finish the job” against Iran unless Tehran changed course. He suggested a different Israeli leader could jeopardise American support. (Axios)

Netanyahu said he had ordered security agencies to prepare a comprehensive plan to overthrow Iran’s leadership. Israel could act independently of Washington if necessary. (Times of Israel)

Araghchi responded to Trump by warning that Tehran also had “unfinished jobs”, accusing Netanyahu of pushing America towards another war. (Araghchi)

Iranian parliament speaker Ghalibaf warned Gulf governments, funds and firms against supplying finance, land or energy to AI/data companies assisting attacks on Iran, threatening enforcement against those that did. (Ghalibaf)

Araghchi reiterated Iran’s seven-day Hormuz proposal: lift the US port blockade and oil sanctions and end regional hostilities; Tehran would reopen the strait on day six, with negotiations beginning on day seven. (RTRS)

The US issued a fresh alert urging Americans to leave Iran immediately, warning that Saudi–Houthi fighting could spread rapidly and that Iran or its proxies could target US interests worldwide. (US Embassy)

Separate US regional alerts warned Americans in the Middle East of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruption amid Iranian and Houthi threats. (State Department)

Hegseth said Saturday the Islamic Republic must decide as soon as possible whether it wants to give up its nuclear ambitions in negotiations or face a devastating US attacka. (Iran International)

Trump told a Kentucky rally Saturday that the Iran operation would end soon, predicting gasoline prices would subsequently fall below their pre-war level. (Iran International)

Iran’s parliament approved Mehrdad Akhlaqi as defence minister Sunday. He warned that any US or Israeli miscalculation would trigger an extensive, unexpected response. (RTRS, AP)

Iran’s security council secretary Mohsen Rezaei said Tehran had prepared a more destructive operational plan for another war, which would not follow the rules Washington and Israel expect. (Iran International)

Gulf foreign ministers said any Iran agreement must address its nuclear, missile, drone and proxy programmes, with GCC participation in negotiations affecting the bloc’s security. (GCC)

The GCC declared that an attack on any member constitutes an attack on all, backing Saudi defensive measures and reaffirming the right to individual and collective self-defence. (GCC)

The IRGC claimed a supertanker carrying over 2m barrels of crude struck a mine and caught fire during an unauthorised Hormuz transit. The vessel and damage were not independently confirmed. (Iran International)

In a separate Sunday statement, the IRGC navy claimed another outbound tanker struck a mine on the southern Hormuz route, causing an engine-room fire. No vessel was named and the claim remained unconfirmed. (Iran International)

A tanker on Saturday 78 nautical miles northeast of Al Jubayl suffered stern damage after an RPG attack from a small boat. The crew were safe. (Iran International)

CENTCOM’s Tim Hawkins said 97% of ships attempting Hormuz passage had crossed without Iranian projectile hits, insisting the strait remained open. (Fox News)

Egypt’s National Defence Council backed military support for Saudi Arabia, with parliamentary authorisation sought. Sisi said any deployment would be defensive and contingent on a Saudi request; no deployment was announced. (FT, The National)

Iran is providing the Houthis with targeting assistance, intelligence and military training for attacks on Saudi Arabia, people briefed on regional intelligence told WSJ. Iranian officers have also helped direct attacks; Iran and the Houthis deny the allegations. (WSJ)

Saudi Arabia is seeking air-defence units and military assistance from Turkey, Pakistan and European countries as interceptor shortages hamper its response. US assistance remains limited to intelligence and other support. (WSJ)

The Saudi-led coalition said on Saturday it intercepted a ballistic missile heading towards the Yanbu oil hub. (RTRS)

China’s September crude processing fell 8.4% y/y to 57.5m tonnes despite improving Gulf shipping conditions, extending pressure on fuel supplies. (BBG)

Japanese spot power prices reached roughly a four-year high of ¥31.15/kWh, up more than 25% over the week. Maintenance reduced available capacity 12% versus a month earlier while coal and LNG costs remain elevated. (BBG)

GEOPOLITICAL:

The Trump administration is proposing renewed Russian pipeline-gas sales to Europe as part of a Ukraine settlement. Kushner and Witkoff have raised restarting routes through Ukraine; European officials have pushed back. (NYT)

Zelenskyy said Starlink remained restricted above roughly 161km/h in Ukraine, impairing interceptor drones and supply missions; tests outside Ukraine worked normally. Rubio denied a US order and said he understood service had resumed, leaving the extent of restoration disputed. (Axios, FT)

Bessent warned Zelenskyy to “be very careful” about accusing the US of deliberately restricting Ukraine’s satellite access. (CNBC)

Trump waived most Russia sanctions and tariff provisions under the Graham law before implementation. The sweeping penalties, including the headline 500% duties, were not being implemented under the order. (White House)

Trump defended the Russian diesel deal and sanctions waiver as a way to keep Putin engaged in peace talks. He also argued Moscow was providing Iran with less assistance than it could and wanted to preserve that restraint. (BBG, Iran International)

At least 10 Republican senators opposed the Russia waiver. Speaker Johnson said he would discuss its consequences with the White House. (BBG)

Putin proposed Ukraine talks with Trump and Xi alongside November 18–19’s APEC summit in Shenzhen, excluding Kyiv and European leaders. Trump has not agreed; Beijing indicated it would not object if he participated. (WSJ)

Ukrainian officials said senior US military leaders warned intelligence cooperation was at risk if Kyiv continued refinery strikes. US officials say sharing continues and attribute recent missed launch warnings to bad weather. (WSJ)

Zelenskyy said Sunday that US intelligence sharing had resumed following a pause. (Reuters)

Zelenskyy offered to stop Russian refinery strikes in exchange for more Patriot interceptors, saying the US was supplying only 12 missiles a month—roughly a quarter of the Biden-era pace. (BBG)

Zelenskyy separately accused the US of delaying authorisation for Patriot supplies already paid for under PURL, saying the hold-up was political rather than technical. (BBG)

Zelenskyy is discussing another meeting with Witkoff and Kushner, potentially this week. The US envoys also plan further Putin talks; the next round has not been confirmed. (BBG)

Zelenskyy said Russia launched more than 320 drones and missiles in one of its largest attacks on Ukraine’s energy sector Saturday. (Zelenskyy)

Ukrainian drones struck the St Petersburg oil terminal Sunday in the city’s biggest attack of the war. Zelenskyy said Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy sector 76 times over the preceding week. (WSJ)

Ukraine is discussing a protected Black Sea grain corridor using Turkish-, Indian- and Egyptian-flagged vessels. Zelenskyy said Russia opposed it and Ukrainian exports were running at 38% of normal levels. (BBG)

Turkey will receive some Russian diesel released under the US arrangement, Energy Minister Bayraktar said. The agreement covers more than 1.8m tonnes globally, with US licensing through April 2027. (Bayraktar remarks)

US ambassador Andrew Puzder warned European companies could face devastating retaliation if Brussels restricts American satellite operators. He also criticised legislation favouring domestic cloud providers. (FT)

Latvian PM Andris Kulbergs called for an EU-wide halt to Russian tourist visas, citing hybrid-attack risks. France has signalled tighter issuance and Italy is open to discussions. (FT)

At least 12 sanctioned tankers appear to be using identical devices to broadcast false Black Sea locations, researchers told the FT. Six simultaneously transmitted two positions, suggesting coordinated concealment of Russian oil shipments. (FT)

US Army Pacific commander Ronald Clark called for more visible American military capability in Asia. He confirmed the US and Cambodia would resume Angkor Sentinel exercises in February after almost a decade. (FT)

EQUITIES:

Microsoft cancelled its lease for Nscale’s entire 50MW Loughton site in the UK after grid power slipped beyond 2030. Nscale is seeking another tenant and alternative power; other Microsoft contracts are unaffected. (FT)

Nscale IPO investors are pushing for a lower $16–19bn valuation versus the company’s roughly $30bn target. Formal marketing has not begun while Nscale addresses SEC comments. (BBG)

Anthropic is offering Blackstone a high yield of more than 10% to finance its latest chip deal, highlighting the start-up’s willingness to stomach steep borrowing costs to finance expensive AI infrastructure. The $60bn debt package, dubbed “Project North Star”, would help fund Anthropic’s procurement of about 1.5 gigawatts of custom semiconductors developed by Google (TPUs). (FT)

Anthropic proposed allocating 5% of its shares to a public-benefit fund, subject to shareholder approval. Including existing founder and employee pledges, approximately 20% of equity would support public benefit; additional allocations would be linked to valuation gains. (Anthropic, FT)

Anthropic signed its first Canadian data-centre lease with EverWind at Point Tupper, Nova Scotia. EverWind’s broader campus and wind-power development is planned to exceed C$10bn. (RTRS)

OpenAI hired SpaceX/xAI sales executive Graham Seamans to lead cybersecurity sales, adding another commercial recruit from Musk’s AI businesses. (BBG)

AWS CFO John Felton said AI server investments generate paybacks under three years, defending capex against a nearly $500bn Q2 backlog. (Axios)

Ben Horowitz said Amazon CEO Andy Jassy told him Amazon’s compute was sold out into late 2028 or beyond. (All-In comments)

JPMorgan upgraded Intel to Neutral from Underweight, PT $85, citing execution, yields and foundry prospects. Its 2028 EPS estimate is roughly 15% above consensus, although server CPU share losses remain a concern. (JPMorgan)

Apple reporter Gurman reports a November 5–6 retail-store reset, pointing to November 6 availability for at least some new Macs and/or the OLED iPad mini after the late-October unveiling. (Bloomberg)

SanDisk announced an exclusive storage partnership for Meta’s VR glasses due next spring, covering microSD Express cards and USB-C flash drives. (The Elec)

Irrational Analysis’s OCP recap says Credo’s plans are shifting from micro-LED towards micro-VCSEL optical links. The author remains bullish; this is their interpretation of presentations and demos. (Irrational Analysis)

Blue Owl bankers have pitched its founders a full or partial sale amid redemption pressure and a roughly 67% share-price decline from January 2025’s high. No sale process was reported. (WSJ)

JPM is launching JPM Coin on Ethereum for institutional clients, extending its dollar-deposit token beyond Base. It supports round-the-clock payments and settlement or collateralisation of tokenised assets. (BBG)

Samsung will reportedly use TSMC’s 3nm process for Nvidia-specific HBM base dies. Nvidia has asked Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron to standardise the design, Seoul Economic Daily reported. (RTRS)

South Korea’s regulator said Solidigm’s proposed US listing could violate dual-listing rules. Authorities await a formal interpretation of whether a domestic securities filing is required. (RTRS)

TSMC’s second Kumamoto fab will produce more advanced wafers than initially planned, Taiwan News reported. (Taiwan News)

Google’s TPU v9 reportedly faces a roughly three-week redesign delay, potentially pushing tape-out to January 2027 and shipments to Q1 2028. November sampling remains targeted, Commercial Times says. Of note for MediaTek. (Commercial Times)

ByteDance is reportedly discussing a custom data-centre chip with MediaTek, potentially adding a supplier alongside Qualcomm. US regulatory approval remains unresolved. (Commercial Times)

SoftBank is Is in early talks to buy G4S owner Allied Universal, potentially for up to $18bn excluding debt or nearly $30bn including it. A deal is uncertain and would extend its AI/robotics security push. (WSJ, FT)

Kioxia leveraged share positions reached roughly ¥920bn, the largest on the Tokyo exchange, while turnover collapsed from its peak. Margin repayment deadlines are raising forced-unwind risks. (BBG)

DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash-1017 across its app, website and API, claiming faster completion, shorter outputs and improvements in reasoning, coding, agentic work and vision. (DeepSeek)

The PRA is examining an insider allegation at Barclays that private-credit risk was understated through trading-book treatment of derivatives linked to illiquid loans. Traders defended the treatment on hedging grounds; Barclays says it takes regulatory obligations seriously. (FT)

Morgan Stanley is entering UK retail savings through Raisin with fixed-term deposit rates up to 5.1%. Sources describe it as deposit funding rather than a broader retail-banking expansion. (BBG)

Hermès is targeting wealthy US suburbs and smaller cities using customer ZIP-code data. Americas revenue grew 15% in H1 versus 2% in Asia excluding Japan. (WSJ)

European airline executives warn persistent fuel costs will force higher fares, smaller fleets and weaker expansion as hedges expire. TAP sees a difficult three to five years; ITA has not added fresh 2027 fuel hedges. (FT)

Workers at Antofagasta’s Centinela mine accepted a wage offer, paving the way to end the October 7 strike once contracts are signed. The two unions represent about 700 workers. (BBG)
