text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

It was a crisp October morning in New York City in 1789 when John Jay stepped forward to take the two solemn oaths that would make him the first Chief Justice of the United States. The city still carried the scars and the energy of the recent war; the new federal government had only just begun to find its footing, and the Supreme Court itself existed more as a promise in the Constitution than as a living institution. Yet there stood Jay—quiet, deliberate, already one of the most widely trusted men of his generation—before Richard Morris, Chief Justice of New York, swearing to administer justice without respect to persons and to support the Constitution of the United States.

Few men were better prepared for the task. Jay had already served as president of the Continental Congress, helped negotiate the Treaty of Paris that secured American independence, guided the nation’s foreign affairs under the Articles of Confederation, and written some of the most persuasive essays in The Federalist. When George Washington offered him the post of Secretary of State, Jay declined; when the President then turned to him for the newly created office of Chief Justice, he accepted. Washington had signed the Judiciary Act only weeks earlier, on September 24. The Senate confirmed Jay two days later. On October 19 he took the oaths, and with that simple ceremony the third branch of government began its long, uncertain life.

The Court that assembled under him the following February in the Merchants Exchange Building was small and largely untested. There were almost no cases at first. The justices would soon face the hard, often lonely work of riding circuit over rough roads, and the prestige of the Court was still something they would have to earn. Jay served six years before resigning to become governor of New York. In those early years, however, he helped establish the expectation that the Court would stand apart from politics and parties, bound by the Constitution and by the oath he had taken on that October day.

In the life of John Jay one sees the character of the generation that made the republic: men who had risked everything in the cause of independence and then turned, with equal seriousness, to the slower work of building lasting institutions. The oath he swore in 1789 was not merely a formality. It was an act of faith in the idea that law, carefully administered, could hold a free people together.

text:
"Vladimir Putin has proposed meeting President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping next month to pursue a Ukraine settlement on terms favorable to Moscow.

The proposed talks would leave Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European leaders outside the negotiations. Trump has not accepted the invitation, a senior U.S. official told the Wall Street Journal.

Moscow has suggested convening the three leaders alongside the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on November 18–19.

Beijing has indicated it would accept the arrangement if Trump agrees, according to people close to discussions between Russian and Chinese officials.

Proposal Remains Preliminary
Putin raised the idea during a telephone call with Trump on October 9, according to a former Russian intelligence officer briefed on the exchange.

The call also led to an agreement for Washington to buy Russian diesel and help market it internationally.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov acknowledged that a possible meeting was under discussion but said neither its format nor its substance had been settled.

“There is no clear understanding yet regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda, although all three parties acknowledge the hypothetical possibility of such a meeting taking place,” he told the Journal.

The senior U.S. official said Trump could consider the proposal as he seeks to deliver on his pledge to end the war. U.S.-brokered peace efforts have made little progress.

The White House declined to comment. China’s embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.

Moscow Seeks Diplomatic Opening
The initiative comes as Washington moves closer to Moscow while relations with Kyiv deteriorate.

Alongside the diesel agreement, Trump on Friday suspended most sanctions that would have taken effect under bipartisan legislation he signed last month.

The decision drew objections from lawmakers, including some Republicans.

A senior White House official said the president saw limited alternatives for reducing fuel prices.

Energy experts, however, identify the Iran war as the main driver of higher diesel costs and expect the promised Russian supplies to have little effect on prices.

Trump has also demanded that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian refineries and suggested it needs a different president.

After Ukrainian forces struck an oil terminal in St. Petersburg on Sunday, Trump accused Zelensky of obstructing peace.

He said Ukraine was withholding sanctions to keep Moscow engaged in negotiations.

“I WANT THIS WAR END!” he wrote on Truth Social.

China Weighs Opportunity and Risk
For Moscow, the proposed format offers recognition as a leading global power while excluding Europe, which the Kremlin regards as an obstacle to securing victory in Ukraine.

The former Russian intelligence officer described Putin’s ambitions as extending to a new arrangement of global spheres of influence, modeled on the Yalta summit.

Beijing could use the meeting to advance Xi’s effort to position China as a diplomatic broker between Washington and Moscow.

Chinese officials nevertheless have reservations about Ukraine talks overshadowing their APEC plans, according to people close to the discussions.

Xi must also balance his support for Putin against China’s economic relationship with Europe.

Hosting negotiations that exclude Kyiv could deepen European concerns over Beijing’s alignment with Moscow and draw China further into the conflict."

"Iran's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on ​the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media ‌outlets on Sunday.

Iran presented its proposal in mid-September after an interim ceasefire collapsed. Tehran later acknowledged receiving a US response but Iran’s security chief said last week negotiations ​have stalled because Washington failed to address all seven conditions for ​reopening the strait.

"Our situation is clear and based on ⁠the seven-days proposal presented to the US. They shared comments which ​we are reviewing, but our proposal is still on the table ​and if there is any honesty on the US part, which there isn't, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious," Araqchi said while in ​Baghdad for a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.

Iran's ​conditions include, among other demands, the lifting of the US blockade on its ports, ‌the ⁠lifting of US sanctions on its oil exports as well as ending hostilities on all regional fronts.

If Washington accepts Tehran's conditions, the strait could reopen within six days, with talks resuming the following day, ​Araqchi said.

A central ​point of ⁠disagreement has been Washington’s insistence on addressing Iran's nuclear programme from the outset.
US Vice President JD Vance said ​earlier this month that Iran must make a "meaningful" reduction ​in ⁠its uranium enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries' eight-month war.

Tehran says negotiations should initially focus on reopening the Strait of ⁠Hormuz, ​which before the war carried about a ​fifth of the global trade in oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), and restoring security ​in the waterway."

text:
What Actually is Base?

Built by Coinbase (@coinbase), Base (@base) is an Ethereum (@ethereum) ethereum:native Layer 2 network designed to make onchain transactions faster and cheaper.

But what does that mean for everyday users?

(1) Base Is Built On Ethereum

Base is not a separate Layer 1 blockchain like Solana (@solana) $SOL or Avalanche (@avax) $AVAX. It processes transactions on its own network while relying on Ethereum for key parts of its security and settlement.

This helps reduce costs without leaving Ethereum's broader ecosystem.

(2) How Does Base Work?

Base launched on the OP Stack, a framework for building Ethereum Layer 2 networks. In February 2026, it announced a move to its own unified tech stack, while staying compatible with the OP Stack specification.

Transactions are processed on Base, while transaction data is published to Ethereum. 

This approach helps the network handle activity without requiring every transaction to be processed directly on Ethereum Mainnet.

(3) What Can You Do On Base?

Base supports a growing range of onchain applications, including:

• Decentralized exchanges for token trading
• DeFi platforms for lending and borrowing
• Stablecoin payments and transfers
• Tokenized stocks (for eligible non-US users)
• NFTs, games, and social applications

Developers can also build applications using familiar Ethereum tools.

(4) Does Base Have Its Own Token?

Not yet. Base does not have a native BASE token, though the team has said it is exploring one. 

No launch has been announced. Users pay gas fees in ETH, which is also used across Ethereum’s main network.

(5) Why Does Base Matter?

Coinbase gives Base a connection to a major crypto exchange and its large user base. The network offers a lower-cost way to access Ethereum-based applications, while developers gain another place to build and reach users.

However, lower fees do not eliminate risks. Smart contract bugs, scams, and bridge vulnerabilities can still lead to losses.

Base brings Ethereum applications to a network designed for cheaper transactions.

STOCK MARKET OVERVIEW
Thanks @grok by xAI 🧙‍♂️

US stock futures are modestly higher this morning (Monday, October 19, 2026), led by Nasdaq, as investors cautiously buy the dip in AI/tech after last week’s selloff, supported by retreating oil prices and stabilizing yields.

Current Futures Levels
As of roughly 5:30–6:00 AM ET (based on recent premarket quotes; levels are indicative and can shift):
Nasdaq 100 Futures: ~29,700–29,770 (+1.0–1.3%)
S&P 500 Futures: ~7,740–7,760 (+0.5–0.8%)
Dow Jones Futures: ~52,220 (+0.0–0.5%, relatively flat)

These reflect a rebound after Friday’s close, when the S&P 500 fell ~1.1% (to ~7,659) and Nasdaq Composite dropped ~2.1% (to ~26,140), with the Nasdaq posting its worst week since June and semiconductors seeing their longest losing streak since 2008.

Why Futures Are at These Levels
AI/tech dip-buying: Investors are tentatively returning to artificial intelligence and chip stocks after heavy selling last week over AI spending concerns, elevated valuations, and financing costs for infrastructure. Nvidia is up >2% premarket; chipmakers are leading. Analysts note the need for clearer monetization of AI revenues relative to spending.
Falling oil prices: Brent and WTI have pulled back from Friday’s multi-month highs (near $110 for Brent), reducing immediate inflation/rate pressure fears.
Stabilizing yields: The 10-year Treasury yield is near ~5.06%.
Overnight catalysts: Better-than-expected Chinese data (Q3 GDP 4.5% vs. 4.4% expected; industrial production and retail sales also beat) provided some support. A busy earnings week (focused on AI names) is in focus.

Oil Prices
WTI crude: ~$98–100/bbl (down roughly 1–3% depending on the exact quote and contract).
Brent crude: ~$108/bbl (down ~1–1.7%).

Prices eased after Friday’s surge on Middle East supply fears. Drivers include the U.S. decision Friday to ease certain sanctions/tariffs on Russia (raising the prospect of increased Russian oil supplies) and signs that Middle East physical supply remains relatively intact despite ongoing attacks. Profit-taking is also evident.

Today’s Potentially Market-Moving Events (October 19)
This is a relatively quiet day for U.S. macro data. Key items:
China data (already released overnight): GDP, industrial production, retail sales, fixed asset investment, and unemployment mostly beat or met expectations (positive for global risk sentiment).
Canada CPI (8:30 AM ET / 12:30 UTC): High-impact release for September. Consensus around +0.2% m/m; prior ~3% y/y. Also BoC Business Outlook Survey later.
US NAHB Housing Market Index (10:00 AM ET): Expected 31 (vs. 32 prior) — low-to-moderate impact.
Other: Various European speeches and lower-tier data. The broader week is quieter on the U.S. macro front before housing starts/permits (Tuesday) and other releases; flash PMIs come Friday.

Earnings today (lighter day, focused on financials/industrials): Before open includes Fifth Third Bancorp (FITB) and Cleveland-Cliffs (CLF). After close includes Steel Dynamics (STLD), W.R. Berkley (WRB), Crown Holdings (CCK), and several banks. Major reports later this week include Netflix and GM (Tuesday), Tesla and Meta (Wednesday), IBM, and others — these will be key for AI sentiment.

Relevant Geopolitical Events
Middle East tensions: Ongoing flare-ups involving Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure (including targeting of the Yanbu export hub and other sites), tanker/mine incidents in the Persian Gulf/Strait of Hormuz area, a Saudi helicopter incident near Yemen, and Iranian-related escalations. Saudi intercepts have limited damage so far; U.S. forces have been escorting oil shipments. Supply is holding near pre-conflict levels, which is contributing to the oil pullback, but risks remain elevated. Egypt has offered support to Saudi Arabia; Iran has floated Hormuz reopening proposals.
Russia/Ukraine: U.S. easing of some Russia sanctions (Friday executive action) is a key oil supply factor. Continued tit-for-tat strikes on energy infrastructure. Ukraine-related diplomacy and legislation (e.g., efforts to block certain deals) remain in play.
Other: Protests in France and parts of Europe have supported some haven flows; broader global risk sentiment is cautious.

Overall tone is a cautious risk-on rebound in U.S. futures, with oil relief helping, but Middle East headlines and this week’s AI-related earnings remain key risks. Levels can move quickly with news.

text:
Anthropic just pledged 5% of its equity to launch a public benefit fund, and Elon Musk immediately chimed in suggesting they should just distribute the shares directly to the public instead. The AI lab set up the fund as a wholly owned LLC, promising the equity won't touch lobbying or politics and will instead support workers displaced by AI.

They even plan to add 2% more equity every time the company's valuation jumps by 50%. Musk didn't offer any real mechanics for how to hand out the shares, but his comment hit right where it hurts.

It puts Anthropic's shiny corporate responsibility move under the spotlight, turning standard PR into a messy debate over who actually benefits from the AI boom. Handing equity straight to everyday people would definitely break tech Twitter faster than any chatbot launch.

text:
Rice farmers in rain-fed areas urged to shift to vegetable production amid El Niño threat

By Leilanie G. Adriano

LAOAG CITY – Rice farmers in Ilocos Norte are being encouraged to consider vegetable production as an alternative source of income amid concerns over the potential impact of the El Niño phenomenon on agricultural production and water availability.

"To avoid crop losses, our farmers should practice crop diversification, plant vegetables that are early-maturing and requires less water to sustain growth,” provincial agriculturist Ma. Teresa Bacnat said in an interview on Monday.

Even before the advent of the very strong El Niño, the Office of the Provincial Agriculture and the Department of Agriculture havea been promoting crop diversification to help farmers manage climate-related risks while exploring additional livelihood opportunities during periods of limited irrigation water.

Bacnat said vegetable production offers an alternative in areas where suitable crops can be grown with available water resources and favorable soil conditions.

Farmers may consider crops such as peanut, mung bean and selected off-season vegetables, depending on local conditions, market demand and access to planting materials.

Through the "Agri Ka Dito" program of the provincial government, farmers and fisherfolk can directly request for farm inputs, machinery, irrigation, livestock assistance, fisheries support, fuel, transportation, and marketing assistance to reduce production costs and ensure food security in the province.

As the province prepares for possible water shortages and prolonged dry spells, agricultural stakeholders are exploring measures to protect farmers' livelihoods and sustain food production.

Interventions include the construction and repair of 107 small farm reservoirs across the province and dredging of approximately 27,431 linear meters of irrigation canals benefiting around 3,231 farmers.

The province has also allocated PHP10.5 million for solar-powered irrigation systems to support high-value crop production. (PNA)

text:
Arsenal Player Ratings vs Nottingham Forest: Madueke Delivers Late Winner as Eze Struggle

Arsenal secured a hard-fought 1-0 victory over Nottingham Forest at the City Ground, with Noni Madueke scoring the decisive goal in the 80th minute. The Gunners struggled to create clear-cut opportunities in a scrappy encounter, registering their first shot on target through Madueke’s deflected strike.

The result moved Mikel Arteta’s side to within three points of Premier League leaders Manchester City. While several defenders impressed, Eberechi Eze endured a difficult afternoon and was substituted at half-time.

Arsenal Player Ratings

David Raya – 7/10

Handled Forest’s crosses and set-pieces confidently while producing several impressive long passes to initiate attacks. He also recorded his fourth clean sheet in seven league appearances.

Ben White – 5/10

Defended competently but lacked his usual attacking influence. His delivery was disappointing, while his combinations with Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard lacked their customary sharpness.

Ezri Konsa – 8/10

Produced an impressive defensive display, recovering quickly after a knock and making an important block. His late recovery run helped divert Delap’s effort away from goal.

Gabriel – 8/10

Dominated defensively, making six clearances and handling dangerous Forest counter-attacks effectively. He also threatened from a corner but failed to convert his headed opportunity.

Riccardo Calafiori – 5/10

Offered little going forward and gave away possession with a poor pass that allowed Forest to launch a dangerous counter-attack. His attacking combinations lacked fluency.

Declan Rice – 7/10

Created an early opportunity for Havertz with an excellent cross but missed a promising chance himself. His outstanding late block to deny Wood proved crucial.

Bruno Guimaraes – 6/10

Brought energy and physicality to midfield, winning eight of his ten duels. Although he attempted to progress the ball, his influence was limited.

Bukayo Saka – 5/10

Helped get Williams booked early and delivered some decent set-pieces, but struggled to create danger from open play. He offered little threat in front of goal.

Martin Odegaard – 6/10

Found it difficult to accelerate Arsenal’s attacking play, frequently dropping deep to collect possession. He produced a clever pass that Rice failed to turn into a goal.

Eberechi Eze – 3/10

Struggled throughout the first half, displaying poor intensity and repeatedly losing possession. He recorded no shots, created no chances and completed no successful dribbles before being substituted.

Kai Havertz – 4/10

Missed Arsenal’s clearest first-half opportunity with a poorly directed header and later fired wide from a tight angle. He otherwise contributed little and conceded a needless free-kick.

Substitutes

Noni Madueke – 8/10

Transformed Arsenal’s attack after replacing Eze at half-time. His direct running unsettled Forest before his deflected strike in the 80th minute secured all three points.

Jurrien Timber – 7/10

Added urgency after replacing White, immediately making a dangerous run and delivering an excellent cutback for Rice. His introduction strengthened Arsenal’s attacking play on the right.

Mikel Merino – 6/10

Helped Arsenal maintain composure during the closing stages and attempted a shot from the edge of the area, which was blocked by a defender.

Viktor Gyokeres – 6/10

Provided a more encouraging contribution after replacing Havertz. He troubled Forest’s defenders with runs behind the back line and worked effectively to hold up possession.

text:
The Dark-Phase Proton Lattice: How Myelin Stores Energy from Light
// MyMitohormesisClock

Sleep remains one of biology’s most persistent enigmas. Organisms from insects to humans enter a state of reduced responsiveness for a substantial fraction of each day, yet the primary reason has never been fully settled. One long-standing idea is that sleep restores the brain’s energy reserves. A 2025 hypothesis paper in Progress in Biophysics and Molecular Biology by Alessandro Maria Morelli, Ann Saada, and Felix Scholkmann offers a concrete biophysical account of how that restoration might occur. Myelin—the multilamellar sheath that wraps axons—functions, they propose, as a proton capacitor. During the dark phase, protons accumulate in the major dense line, bound to myelin basic protein and domains of proteolipid protein. During the light phase those protons are released through embedded FoF1-ATP synthase, generating ATP that can enter the axon.

The proposal rests on structural and experimental observations. The major dense line is only a few nanometers wide and densely packed with basic residues capable of holding protons without releasing them into bulk water. Isolated myelin vesicles can retain an energy charge after exposure to NADH and later convert it to ATP. Mitochondrial-derived vesicles supply a plausible route by which respiratory-chain components reach the compacted sheath. Oleamide, an endogenous compound that accumulates with wakefulness, closes gap junctions and thereby favors proton accumulation over continuous discharge. An order-of-magnitude calculation shows that the protons moved by myelin oxygen consumption over roughly eight hours are comparable to the estimated buffering capacity of the proteins and phospholipid head-groups in one cubic centimeter of sheath. Across mammals, white-matter volume scales inversely with the fraction of the day spent asleep, consistent with greater storage capacity reducing the required dark interval.

These elements form a coherent local mechanism. They do not, however, address the origin of the protons themselves or the conditions that determine whether the lattice can be built and stably charged. From first principles the protons are the conserved positive charge that appears when reducing equivalents are oxidized. Those reducing equivalents are the residual of earlier photon-driven charge separation. Photons of specific wavelengths and arrival rates excite chromophores in the retina, skin, and within cells; the resulting electron displacements set both the supply of NADH and the membrane potential that governs how many functional respiratory complexes are packaged into vesicles and delivered to myelin. The dark-phase filling interval therefore cannot be understood in isolation from the photon field that precedes and surrounds it.

The lattice is not a fixed chemical tank. Infrared and near-infrared photons that penetrate tissue alter hydrogen-bond lifetimes and the orientational order of interfacial water. Those changes shift the effective affinity of the lysine, arginine, serine, and threonine groups that hold the protons, so both capacity and leakage rate remain optically tunable after the electrons have been transferred. Residual photons that reach the head during the nominal dark phase can re-excite the same chromophores, reopen segments of the proton wires, and permit slow back-leakage. The fidelity of the store is the integral of photon contrast across the full cycle, not a binary gate closed by oleamide.

text:
You've probably seen the video. A young Frenchwoman in Paris, in tears, begging looters to stop. "Why are you doing this? That's not what we stand for."

Some accounts are mocking her. "She voted for it."

I won't. Because what you see on her face is not stupidity. It's a disease that has infected the entire West, and it has a name: suicidal empathy.

The term comes from Gad Saad, an evolutionary behavioral scientist at Concordia University in Montreal. A man who fled the Lebanese civil war as a child, and who knows what it looks like when a society falls apart. His new book, Suicidal Empathy: Dying to Be Kind, is the follow-up to The Parasitic Mind. Here is the thesis, and why it concerns every one of us.

Empathy is one of the best things about us. It evolved for a reason: to care for our children, our kin, our tribe. It was calibrated for a world where the people you felt for were the people around you, and where empathy always came paired with its counterweight: the instinct to protect your own and to recognize a threat.

Suicidal empathy is what happens when that mechanism misfires. When it fires at the wrong targets, in the wrong amounts, with no brake. When we feel more for the criminal than for his victim. More for the stranger who breaks the rules than for the citizen who follows them. More for how compassionate we look than for what our compassion actually produces.

Where does it come from? Four layers.

First, biology. Empathy is a spotlight, as the psychologist Paul Bloom put it. It lights up the one face in front of you and leaves everything else in the dark. The crying migrant on the boat is visible. The thousands of future victims of a broken system are statistics. A spotlight is a terrible tool for running a country.

Second, our own civilization. The West is the civilization that put the victim at the center of its morality. Christianity taught us to care for the stranger, the poor, the weak. It was one of the greatest moral revolutions in history. But cut off from its other half, justice, responsibility, the duty to protect your own, it turns into something else.

Third, ideology. In The Parasitic Mind, Saad described idea pathogens, ideas that hijack our reasoning. Suicidal empathy is the emotional counterpart: an ideology that hijacks our compassion. It sorts the world into oppressors and victims, then demands unlimited empathy for whoever ranks as the victim, whatever they do.

Fourth, status. In the age of social media, empathy has become a display. Posting "refugees welcome" costs nothing and earns applause. The bill goes to someone else: the working class, the suburbs, the women walking home at night.

The results are everywhere. Criminals treated as victims of society. Sexual assaults by migrants met with lenient sentences. Self-defense branded as aggression. Borders treated as cruelty. Saad's conclusion is simple: a society dies when it would rather display infinite tolerance than use its survival instinct.

Now the part I'll add myself, and that few people dare to say.

On average, women score higher than men on measures of empathy. It's one of the most consistent findings in psychology, across cultures, and it makes perfect evolutionary sense: for most of human history, the survival of children depended on it. It's a strength.

But it means an ideology that weaponizes empathy will hit women harder. And the data shows it: in country after country, young women have moved sharply to the left of young men, especially on immigration.

This is where men have a responsibility.

Not to mock. Not to lecture. Not to say "she deserved it." Empathy has always needed a counterweight, and that counterweight was the protective instinct: the one that draws lines, says no, and stands between the threat and the people it loves.

Men abandoned that role. They were told it was toxic, and many believed it. So they stayed silent at the dinner table, at work, with their partners, sisters, daughters and friends.

That has to end. Men have to have this conversation, honestly and with respect: compassion that cannot say no is not compassion. It's surrender. And the first to pay for it are women.

Many women already understand this better than anyone. Some of the bravest voices in this fight are women, precisely because they are the first to feel the danger in the street.

A civilization rests on a balance: compassion and strength, openness and borders, mercy and justice. When one side swallows the other, the foundations crack. What we are watching in Europe is what happens when empathy has no counterweight left.

Look at that young woman again. She isn't the enemy. She's what this ideology made of a generation that was told kindness would be enough.

Our job is to make sure she's the last generation that has to learn it this way.

Hollywood spent $70 million on two separate reboots over five years to prove what fans already knew: Hellboy without Guillermo del Toro and Ron Perlman is dead on arrival.

Now, Perlman is putting the pressure directly back on the studios. The 76-year-old actor confirmed to Deadline that his standing offer to finish the trilogy with del Toro has no expiration date, even if it takes another decade of prosthetic hell.

The unresolved ending of 2008’s The Golden Army remains one of modern cinema’s biggest cliffhangers. Del Toro had mapped out a biblical, Greek-epic finale revolving around Liz Sherman’s unborn twins and Big Red’s prophetic destiny to trigger the apocalypse in order to save mankind.

Universal balked at the required $120 million budget back in 2012, shelving the auteur vision to save cash. Instead, studios flushed money down the drain on David Harbour’s disastrous 2019 flop ($44M domestic haul on a $50M budget) and 2024’s straight-to-digital The Crooked Man.

When asked if he and del Toro have recently held private talks to finally shoot the trilogy-capper, Perlman delivered a cagey, three-word response: "No comment."

text:
Critics are always quick to place all the blame for Germany's catastrophic military losses on Hitler. But it is easy to judge historical decisions with the benefit of hindsight. In 1941, the outcome of the war was far from certain.

Consider the numbers: Germany had lost approximately 459,000 military personnel by the end of 1941. Had Germany achieved a decisive VICTORY and ended the war that year, its military losses could have remained around that figure. Remarkably, 3.34 million German soldiers died in 1944–1945 alone.

I highly recommend Hitler's Panzers East by R. H. S. Stolfi. He argues that Army Group Center possessed sufficient strength to capture Moscow and potentially defeat the Soviet Union in 1941. Instead, Hitler diverted forces toward Ukraine, sacrificing momentum in what Stolfi considers a potentially war-winning campaign.

There is another factor worth considering: the Allied demand for UNCONDITIONAL surrender, formally announced at the Casablanca Conference in January 1943. This effectively ruled out a negotiated peace that would have allowed the Nazi regime to remain in power.

Under those circumstances, it is hardly surprising that Hitler continued fighting. When surrender offers no possibility of a political compromise, the incentive to keep resisting becomes much stronger, even as the military situation deteriorates.

🇾🇪🇸🇦|Satellite images reveals more than just damage to a single facility. It offers a glimpse into the logic of war: an army that has been warned, a civilian population that has been given advance notice, and a strategic asset that was abandoned well before the air raid sirens even sounded.

A Targeted Site: Not Merely a Military Facility, but the Fuel Hub of Northern Yemen

Before launching the strike, the Saudi led coalition publicly called for civilians to evacuate the Al-Sabaha central fuel depot. The coalition justified the action by claiming the facility was being used to support military operations targeting sites within Saudi Arabia and commercial shipping in the Red Sea.

However, the site slated for evacuation was a fuel distribution hub with a storage capacity of approximately 58,000 metric tons. As one of the Yemen Petroleum Company’s primary storage points in Sanaa, containing at least 200,000 liters of fuel across four major storage tanks, it served as a critical supply source for the capital and its surrounding areas.

While Saudi Arabia classified it as a facility used to support military operations, the Yemen Petroleum Company denied that any petroleum products were stored there, asserting that it held no military value. Satellite imagery captures the physical reality of this contest over definitions: the fuel depot lies in ruins, with dark oil stains spreading around the damaged infrastructure, clear evidence that stored fuel had leaked.

Satellite Imagery Documents Systematic Dismantling, Not Collateral Damage

Open source analysis by Al Jazeera, comparing imagery from before and after the strike, shows rubble scattered across the Al-Sabaha central fuel depot, with clear damage to facilities located south of the main storage tanks.

What is truly significant is not any single crater, but the pattern of the strikes: multiple fuel handling units within the depot were destroyed, and dark patches caused by leaking petroleum products have appeared around the damaged structures. This indicates that the operation was not a surgical strike on an isolated tank, but a systematic targeting of the complex’s fuel distribution nodes, the very hubs responsible for channeling fuel to gas stations, hospital generators, water pumps, and commercial transport systems throughout Sanaa.

The timing of the strike was equally precise. The coalition carried out strikes following an evacuation warning. Yemeni sources reported two civilian deaths and two injuries. Although civilians had been advised to vacate a fuel facility slated for destruction, residents of Sanaa flocked to gas stations even after the warning was issued, fully aware that the facility’s destruction would disrupt their access to fuel for vehicles, power generators, and cooking gas.

The Logic of the 72 Hour Warning: The Silence of the American Umbrella

This strike occurred amidst a recurring cycle of warning, strike, and retaliation. Following the Saudi led coalition’s evacuation warning, the Houthis issued their own advisory, urging employees and civilians near Saudi Aramco facilities to evacuate. They explicitly identified Aramco’s facilities in Dammam, King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, and the Riyadh oil refinery as potential targets.

Hours later, the Saudi led coalition claimed to have intercepted three cruise missiles and two drones aimed at the Riyadh region and southern Saudi Arabia. However, falling debris still resulted in at least four injuries. Simultaneously, an administrative building at an Aramco site in Dhahran, in the Eastern Province, was struck, sparking a contained fire.

The core issue exposed by this cycle is not the Houthis’ strike capability, but rather the ineffectiveness of the protection promised by the United States when it comes to fixed strategic infrastructure. Al-Sabaha is a large, stationary, and well known fuel complex. It is neither a mobile launcher nor an underground bunker, nor is it a target that is difficult to locate. It is a fuel depot situated on the hills west of Sanaa, overlooking the capital.

The United States maintains a military presence in the region, facilitates intelligence sharing, and coordinates air defense. Yet, this facility, the largest fuel distribution hub in northern Yemen, was nonetheless destroyed, with traces of fuel leakage clearly visible in satellite imagery. While the U.S. can share intelligence and coordinate air defenses, it remains unable to prevent the systematic dismantling of a large, fixed, civilian oriented fuel facility. When the object to be protected is a fuel distribution network that must remain in constant operation, rather than a mobile military target, the very concept of protection is reduced to a mere post hoc explanation for why it failed to be protected.

More than just a gas station was destroyed

Satellite imagery of Al-Sabaha captures a node in Sana’a’s fuel supply chain that was surgically excised. This node served as a vital link for the capital’s gas stations, backup generators for hospitals, irrigation pumps, and the livelihoods of transport workers.

The Saudis labeled the facility as one that supports military operations. The Yemen Petroleum Company stated that it contained no fuel, yet satellite imagery shows evidence of a fuel leak. Regardless of how history ultimately records the accounts of either side, the residents of Sana’a are already forming queues in front of gas stations.

Long live Yemen. Long live Ansar Allah. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

Rio Tinto has dodged two 'bullets' due to Glencore's rejection of a merger proposal: a possible BHP takeover bid and a dangerous acquisition. News/Snapshot

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

M&A Activity: Major merger talks continue between giants like Rio Tinto and Glencore as they seek to consolidate copper exposure for the EV market.

Workforce Challenges: The Minerals Council of Australia is currently calling for migration reforms to address a significant "skills crunch" in the sector.

text:
France’s Forgotten Sovereign: The Individual

France educates its young, then makes it so expensive to employ them—that it undermines the future it promises them.

In France, high taxes, social charges and excessive regulation make it unnecessarily costly to build a business, expand or hire. In addition, stringent rules that make existing jobs difficult to end can make new ones difficult to offer.

As a result, young people face fewer opportunities to earn, gain experience and become independent. 

Their frustration is justified.

By consequence, the French state then faces demands to support the very people whose opportunities its own policies have helped restrict.

Less opportunity. More dependence. More spending. More pressure to tax the work and enterprise financing it.

When anger turns into destruction, the circle tightens. Businesses lose capital and income. Public infrastructure must be rebuilt. The bill returns to taxpayers through more taxation, more debt or cuts elsewhere.

A vicious cycle of wealth destruction.

At the core of this debacle lies a disregard for individual sovereignty: the right to direct one’s own life, labour and resources, enter voluntary agreements and retain the fruits of one’s effort.

The libertarian answer begins here: your life, your body, your labour and the fruits of your effort belong to you.

Life, liberty and property give substance to independence. They allow people to shape their lives, see their efforts matter and create value for others.

As long as France keeps making that independence harder to achieve, while expanding the dependence it must finance, the cycle will continue.

text:
Connecting the Thread

Our recent entries have followed Christianity through the increasingly bitter religious conflicts of Tudor England.

William Tyndale died defending Protestant teachings. Thomas Cranmer helped establish Protestant reforms before being executed under a Catholic monarch. Margaret Clitherow suffered under a Protestant government for protecting Catholic priests.

Thomas More adds another dimension: the Christian statesman who served royal authority until he believed obedience would violate his obligations to God.

His resistance belongs to a much older tradition.

Early Christian martyrs refused imperial commands to sacrifice to pagan gods. Medieval churchmen challenged kings who attempted to control ecclesiastical institutions. More confronted a Christian monarch claiming supreme authority over the national Church.

Yet the religious persecutions of the Reformation also exposed the limitations of those earlier arguments.

If conscience mattered when a Catholic resisted a Protestant king, why should it not matter when a Protestant resisted a Catholic queen?

That question would become increasingly urgent during the English religious conflicts of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

Later developments in constitutional government, religious toleration, and the American founding drew upon many influences, including Christian understandings of conscience, English legal traditions, Enlightenment philosophy, and the experience of religious persecution.

The resulting protections for religious liberty went considerably beyond what More himself advocated.

Early Christian Martyrs → Medieval Church and Crown → Thomas Becket → Thomas More → English Reformation → Religious Persecution and Toleration → English Constitutional Development → American Religious Liberty

There is a final distinction worth remembering.

More did not deny that Henry VIII was his king.

He did not organize an armed rebellion or attempt to overthrow the government.

He maintained that there was a boundary beyond which his obedience could not extend.

The tragedy is that he had not consistently recognized an equivalent boundary when exercising authority over religious dissenters.

His life therefore offers both an example of extraordinary personal courage and a warning about the responsibilities that accompany power.

Thomas More was willing to die rather than betray his conscience. His story challenges later generations to protect that same principle even for those whose convictions they believe are mistaken.

text:
Scottish Statehood and the Law https://t.co/rhFZ2Sm4V7 
Partnership or annexation

The state – the international person – recognised in international law in which this conference is taking place, is the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. If a part of the territory of that international person – Scotland for example – wished to become independent how, in law, could that come about? The answer to that question depends on how one classifies the process whereby the currently recognised international legal person came into existence.

As every schoolchild knows, before May 1707, the island of Britain was divided into two independent nations: Scotland in the north, and England in the south. The orthodox view is that these two states entered an international agreement, followed by Acts of their respective parliaments. By mutual consent, both ceased to exist, merging into a voluntary partnership to be reborn as a single unitary state: the United Kingdom of Great Britain.

If the orthodox view is correct, if Scotland and England both ceased to exist and a new state, Great Britain, rose phoenix-like from their ashes, then the only internationally recognised means for Scotland to become independent would be to secede from that new state. And secession requires the consent of the state being seceded from. That is the view of the current situation unsurprisingly taken by the UK Government. It is also, more surprisingly, the view taken by the Scottish Parliament and the Scottish Government, as shown by repeatedly asking Westminster for a section 30 Order to allow a referendum on independence and repeatedly being refused or brushed off with “now is not the time” (and we’ll decide when the time is, if ever) or “once in a generation” (and we’ll decide how long a generation is).

If you simply look at paperwork, at the Treaty and the Acts of the Scottish and English parliaments, then the orthodox view appears unanswerable. But what if the paperwork disguises or misrepresents what the true nature of the transaction was? This is known in legal circles as the concept of simulation: where legal forms are used to disguise the true nature of the underlying transaction. Names and descriptions in documents do not necessarily determine the legal reality. If England continued in existence while absorbing Scotland, calling the enlarged state Great Britain does not make England disappear any more than changing a company's name necessarily creates a new legal person.

So what is the position if the true legal characterisation of what happened in 1707 was not the creation of a new state through the voluntary partnership of two states which then each simultaneously committed suicide, but was rather the absorption of one of the pre-existing states by the other – that other remaining in existence, wholly unchanged save for the extension of its geographical boundaries?

In that case if Scotland sought once again to become an independent state the branch of international law which governs is not the law of secession but the law relating to resumption or recovery of sovereignty after annexation or colonisation. Modern examples of this process can be seen in the case of Namibia and the Baltic Republics of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. This branch of international law does not require the consent of the annexing state, indeed prohibits the annexing state’s interference in the process whereby the annexed state seeks to demonstrate that its inhabitants truly desire to resume independent sovereignty. 

The absolutely crucial legal issue accordingly is whether the state in which this conference is being held was a new state born in 1707 through a voluntary partnership between Scotland and England whereby both ceased to exist as states in international law, or whether, under cover of documents talking of or envisaging partnership and a new state, what actually happened was that England remained in existence and simply annexed or absorbed Scotland. 

So that is what it boils down to: is Scotland a voluntary partner in a unitary state jointly created by itself and England in 1707; or is Scotland an annexed territory of a continued and continuing England, cosmetically renamed Great Britain? If it is an annexed territory, then in law independence is achieved not through secession, but through recovery or resumption of sovereignty. 

Some Scots have an instinctive reluctance to accept the characterisation of Scotland as a colony of or as a dependency of England. Perhaps they might accept or find more palatable the description of Scotland as a territory annexed by England. In international law it’s the same thing and the consequences of the characterisation are the same.

In my talk to this conference last year I explained how, to my own considerable surprise, I had come to the conclusion, looking at the organs of government of the post-1707 state, that for England nothing changed. What occurred was a takeover of Scotland by England, not a voluntary partnership or merger creating a new legal entity. As a state, England continued; Scotland did not. The conclusion which I then reached is reinforced by manifold instances in which it was simply assumed by authorities of the new regime – taken for granted – that English law, procedure and institutions extended to Scotland and to Scots post-1707. Here are a few examples.

1. A very telling symbol of this continuity of England is the title adopted by the late Queen, as proclaimed with the advice of the UK Government on her accession to the throne in 1952. That title was “Elizabeth the Second” notwithstanding the fact that the first Elizabeth, Elizabeth Tudor, reigned over England alone. Had a new state replacing England come into existence in 1707, the late queen would have been the first monarch with the name of Elizabeth to be its head of state. The use of "the Second" is a quiet but profound admission that the English monarchy, and by extension, the English state, continued undisturbed. Similarly, had a new state really come into existence in 1707 the king who succeeded George IV in 1830 would have been William I, not William IV, and the two twentieth century kings entitled Edward VII and Edward VIII would have been Edward I and Edward II.

2. The first official collection of the legislation of the Westminster parliament, The Statutes of the Realm was published between 1810 and 1822. In that collection the numbering (by regnal year and chapter number) of the legislation passed by the Parliament continued in an unbroken series before and after the addition of the Scottish members. Thus, the Act of the English Parliament ratifying the Treaty of Union was 6 Anne c11; the last Act passed by it before the new dispensation took effect on 1 May 1707 was 6 Anne c34 (An Act for continuing the laws relating to the poor, and to the buying and selling of cattle in Smithfield and for suppressing of piracy); and the first Act passed after the addition of Scottish members was numbered 6 Anne c35 (Land Tax Act). For England, nothing changed. It was only when a new collected edition of legislation Statutes at Large was published between 1870 and 1878 that the numbering system was changed and Acts passed after the admission of Scots to the English Parliament were re-numbered as starting with 6 Anne c1. And the volumes of the official History of Parliament (covering England from 1264 onwards) have no volume breaks for the Houses of Commons and Lords at 1707, they simply blithely carry on from their previous treatment of the English Parliament.

3. In the Union with Ireland Act 1800 (c67), almost 100 years after the supposed establishment of the new state of Great Britain, the section which narrates the terms of the union is headed “The Parliaments of England and Ireland have agreed on the articles following”.

4. In the Strathmore Peerage Case in the House of Lords in 1821 (6 Pat 645 at 655) Lord Redesdale said: “If your Lordships will look at the Act of Union you will perceive that nothing is stipulated with respect to the continuance of the laws of England; but it is evident, and it has always been conceived, that the law of England was thenceforth to be deemed the general law of the realm of Great Britain (...) except as qualified by the particular provision with respect to the laws of Scotland” (presumably Article 18). He had earlier described the law of Scotland as “the peculiar laws of a particular district”.

5. Acts of the pre-Union parliaments of both Scotland and England provided for Scottish or English nationality to be conferred on certain classes of foreigners if they chose to claim it. A Scots Act of 1695 (c88) provided that a foreigner holding a minimum of £1000 Scots in stock of the Bank of Scotland was entitled to claim Scottish citizenship. In 1818 a national of China who worked in Edinburgh claimed citizenship in reliance on this provision. The UK government objected. The case went through the Court of Session all the way to the House of Lords (Macao v Officers of State 14 Nov 1820 FC) where Lord Redesdale opined: “It is perfectly clear that the Court of Session had no jurisdiction on the subject of such an action as this … The public law is that which is the law of the whole country (...) the public law of the whole empire” whereas the law of Scotland was the law of a “local jurisdiction that can have no power to act with respect to public law”. On the facts of the actual case, the decision may seem reasonable enough: after all, what was being claimed was post-1707 British citizenship, not Scottish citizenship. However, exactly the same question arose in the middle of the 20th century in the English courts. An English Act of 1705 provided for citizenship of England to be conferred on descendants of Electress Sophia of Hanover should they choose to claim it. After World War II a descendant of Sophia, Prince Ernest Augustus (who, incidentally, had fought for Germany in the war) claimed British citizenship in reliance on this Act. His case too went up to the House of Lords (Attorney-General v Prince Ernest Augustus of Hanover [1957] AC 436) and his claim to British citizenship, unlike Mr Macao’s, succeeded there. There can hardly be a clearer or more authoritative legal statement than this that England continued in existence after 1707, whereas Scotland did not. An English Act passed before Union could still operate as the basis for British nationality centuries later. Here you have the highest court in the land by its decision implicitly recognising that what existed after 1707 was a continuation of English nationality, not the creation of a new one. The institutional assumption clearly was: English law continued and applied throughout the whole realm; Scottish law was localised.

6. After 1707 the law which followed colonists to colonies in which they settled was always English law, even in cases where the colonists in question were exclusively or predominantly Scottish. An Australian authority (R T E Latham, 1949) commented: “ It is remarkable that after the … Union with Scotland in 1707 … the law that followed citizens of the united realm to colonies subsequently founded was invariably the law of England. There is nothing in the Acts of Union or elsewhere expressly providing this.”  And a Canadian lawyer (J E Côté, 1977) wrote: “Large as the Scots have bulked in the history of the British Empire, no one has ever doubted that it was purely English law that was introduced into such colonies. That is true even of Nova Scotia …” 

I submit that the explanation is simple: the state of which post-1707 colonists were citizens was England, cosmetically renamed Great Britain after its annexation of Scotland, and so it was the law of England that accompanied them. 

Much of this happened unthinkingly: it was simply inconceivable to those exercising authority that the English law and practice with which they were familiar should not automatically now apply throughout the whole island. In some instances, however, the extension to Scotland was deliberate and far from unthinking. This is most clearly seen in the Treason Act 1708, which applied the English law of treason to Scotland. This was highly technical law based on judicial interpretation of an Act of 1351 in the reign of Edward III. Scots who participated in the 18th century risings were usually sent to England to be tried for treason even if the treasonable acts alleged occurred in Scotland. And as late as 1820 special commissions of Oyer and Terminer were sent from London to try Scotsmen on treason charges in Scotland, with an English prosecutor to keep the court right on the English law of treason.

The meaning of Scottish sovereignty

If what happened in 1707 was that Scotland was annexed by and absorbed into a still subsisting England, what was it of value that the Scots people lost and that would, or at least could, be regained if Scotland recovered or resumed its statehood? The primary answer to this question is, of course, sovereignty.  In England the constitutional doctrine, at least after the deposition of James II in 1688, was (and remains today} that sovereignty reposes in the King in Parliament. In shorthand this is referred to simply as parliamentary sovereignty: Parliament can make or unmake any law whatsoever. In Scotland, on the other hand, sovereignty was said to repose with the people. But what did this actually mean? Was it really any more than performative posturing? Luckily we have a Scottish constitutional law textbook dating from 1579 that gives us answers to these questions: De Jure Regni Apud Scotos by George Buchanan.

Buchanan argued that ultimate political power and sovereignty reside with the people, not the monarch. Drawing on Aristotelian naturalism and early social contract theory, he asserted that the first Scottish society voluntarily created a monarchy out of the laws of nature to maintain order. Therefore, the king’s authority is not absolute or divine, but a delegated trust. 

Buchanan claimed that, by historical precedent, the Scottish crown was fundamentally elective and conditional. He pointed to the coronation oath as a legally binding compact. When Scottish kings were inaugurated, they made a solemn promise to the people to uphold the laws and ancient practices of their ancestors. If the king fails to meet these conditions, the mutual bond between the ruler and the citizens is dissolved. 

A fundamental pillar of Buchanan's constitutional theory is that the king is subject to the law, not above it. Buchanan argued that because a king who becomes a tyrant breaks the constitutional social contract, they forfeit their right to rule and effectively become a public enemy to the state. Consequently, the community has a lawful right to resist, put on trial, depose, or even punish the monarch. 

We see these ideas being expressed in Scotland both before and after George Buchanan’s time, eg in the 1310 Declaration of the Clergy in favour of Robert the Bruce who “with the concurrence and consent of the people he was chosen to be King”; and in the Declaration of Arbroath in 1320: “Divine Providence (...) the law and customs of the kingdom (which we will defend till death) and the due and lawful consent and assent of all the people made him our king and prince. To him we are obliged and resolved to adhere in all things, both on account of his right and his own merit, as being the person who hath restored the people’s safety in defence of their liberties. But after all, if this prince shall leave these principles he hath so nobly pursued, and consent that we or our kingdom be subjected to the king or people of England, we will immediately endeavour to expel him, as our enemy and as the subverter both of his own and our rights, and we will make another king, who will defend our liberties.”

The Claim of Right, 100 years after Buchanan’s time, was to a large extent founded on the constitutional principles that he had enunciated: James VII had breached the terms of his contract with the Scottish people, who had therefore exercised their right to depose him and to offer the throne to William and Mary. The English equivalent document, the Bill of Rights 1689 is founded upon a quite different thesis: James II had abdicated the throne and fled the country, thereby opening the door to Parliament offering the English Crown to someone else.

However, popular sovereignty under the Claim of Right, following Buchanan, does not simply consist of the high constitutional principle that the people of Scotland have the legal right to remove kings who fail in their legal duties to the people. It goes much beyond that. It entails that the people (“to whom belongs the supreme power” Buchanan, p99) make the law and that the king, or head of state, is bound by the law so made. 

It was always the case that Acts of the Parliament of Scotland applied to the king as much as to the citizenry. Compare this with England, where an Act of Parliament did not bind the monarch unless it was specifically stated in it that it did. The Claim of Right goes on to state that all proclamations asserting absolute power to cass, annul and disable laws are contrary to law. This applies to parliaments as well as to kings. It is the people, not the king and not the parliament who are sovereign. 

Furthermore, in Scotland, unlike England, legislation could simply expire by desuetude – through the people simply not accepting it and continuing to act contrary to its terms. An interesting example of this is the 1424 Act of James I prohibiting the playing of football, a game which I understand is still being played after a fashion in Scotland today.  

John Erskine of Carnock, one of my most distinguished predecessors as Professor of Scots Law at Edinburgh University, in his Institutes (I. i. 45, 1773) wrote “... as a posterior statute may repeal or derogate from a prior, so posterior custom may repeal or derogate from a prior statute … for the contrary custom sufficiently presumes the will of the community to alter the law in all its clauses … and this presumed will of the people operates as strongly as their express declaration.”  That is a truly remarkable constitutional idea. The people do not merely obey the law. The law ultimately derives its authority from the community, from the people; and by consistently disregarding and acting contrary to a particular legislative provision, they effectively repeal it. The people, not the king and legislature, are sovereign.

Common good in burghs and regalia nationally

Popular sovereignty is also demonstrated in the Scots law relating to public property, both local and national. The common good property held by local authorities today originates in the common good of a burgh, a concept which has existed for more than 500 years, as the following extract (still in force) from the Common Good Act 1491 demonstrates: “Item it is statut and ordinit that the commoune gud of all our souerane lordis burrowis within the realme be obseruit and kepit to the commoune gude of the toune and to be spendit in commoune and necessare thingis of the burght be the avise of the consale of the toune for the tyme and dekkynnis of craftis quhare thai ar” (1491 c36, s 1). [see Mark Lazarowicz, 2023 Journal of the Law Society of Scotland]

As regards national public property Erskine wrote (Inst II vi 17): “All the subjects which were by the Roman law accounted res publicae are held to be inter regalia or in patrimonio principis, as rivers, free ports, and highways leading from one city, borough, public port or ferry to another … But as the regalia of this sort are … chiefly adapted to public use, the king’s right in them is truly no more than a trust for behoof of his people.” These regalia are “inseparable from the royal dignity and are incommunicable [ie untransferable] absolutely and without exception” or at least are not communicable without the interposition of the states of the kingdom (Inst II vi 13).

The liberty of the citizen

The Claim of Right’s constitutional reach extends far beyond the position of the head of state and the legislature and limitations on their power. It contains what can today be regarded as the core protections of the liberties of the citizen. According to the Claim of Right, the following are all contrary to law:

Extraordinary fines, exorbitant bail, arresting without stating reason, fines and forfeitures before sentence, delaying trial;

Causing pursuit and depriving of rights/property of persons upon stretches of old and obsolete laws, upon frivolous and weak pretences, upon lame and defective probations;

Interfering with the self-government of burghs;

Trying to influence courts by private approaches;

Self-incrimination, torture;

Holding it to be treason for persons to refuse to disclose their private thoughts and judgements in relation to points of treason or other men’s actions.

There are further provisions outlawing martial law in times of peace, the billetting soldiers in private households and, most importantly, prohibiting husbands being penalised for the failure of their wives to attend church. 

Here, then, derived from a 16th century Scottish textbook and a 17th century Scottish legislative statement we have the bare bones of a constitution, including a bill of rights, for a revived nation state of Scotland. 

What was lost in 1707?

What did the people of Scotland lose through its annexation and absorption? Not merely a parliament. Not merely a government. Not merely international personality. The fundamental loss was of the institutional mechanisms for giving effect to the exercise of Scottish popular sovereignty.

Scotland lost control over its constitutional development. It lost control over its economic development and its natural resources. Some local institutions, of course, survived. But these were surviving Scottish institutions within a state whose central political machinery was no longer Scottish.

A constitution for a revived sovereign Scotland

In George Buchanan’s treatise and in the Claim of Right we have material upon which a modern constitution can be built. Of course, these bare bones would require to be fleshed out; but there are many modern 20th and 21st century constitutions which can be studied for inspiration, including those of South Africa, Namibia, Tuvalu, Zimbabwe and Zambia. And constitution-building is a task that all of us who are serious about Scotland recovering her statehood should be quite urgently engaged upon. Because resumption of Scotland’s statehood is coming, and when it does we are likely in retrospect to assess that it happened “gradually and then suddenly” or, as Ernest Hemingway’s words are more usually misquoted, “slowly, then all at once”. 

Robert Black KC FRSE

18 October 2026

The value of Alphabet’s stake in the artificial intelligence start-up Anthropic has soared to around $US124 billion ($178 billion), making it one of the most lucrative bets in the company’s history.The Google parent disclosed in a filing on Thursday (Friday AEST) that the value of its investments in unidentified private companies totalled roughly $US124.3 billion as of June 30. The filing noted that this value is “primarily” driven by one investment, which is a reference to Alphabet’s stake in Anthropic, according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The company said it recorded about $US77 billion in unrealised gains from its private investments in the second quarter, without providing further details in the filing. Google has emerged as one of Anthropic’s biggest backers over the past several years. The technology giant first invested $US3 billion in the start-up starting in 2023. Earlier this year, it agreed to invest as much as $US40 billion more, consisting of $US10 billion upfront and a potential $US30 billion in additional funding tied to operational and financial milestones through 2030.Alphabet’s filing on Thursday showed the remaining commitment has fallen to $US20 billion as of June 30 from $US30 billion at the end of the first quarter, suggesting that Google invested another $US10 billion in the start-up last quarter. Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Uranium Rally: Prices exceeding US$100/lb have sparked renewed interest in Australian prospects like the Kalkaroo project.

text:
Examining U.S. Marriage and Divorce Trends: Highest Rates, Alabama's Ranking

Family formation and marital dynamics vary significantly across the United States, shaped by regional culture, median age at marriage, and demographic shifts. A comprehensive report published by Visual Capitalist, drawing on U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey data, highlights striking state-by-state contrasts in where Americans are getting married and divorced. So where does Alabama rank?

According to the Census Bureau analysis featured by Visual Capitalist, annual divorce rates per 1,000 residents aged 15 and older show distinct regional clustering:

Oklahoma leads the nation with the highest divorce rate, recording 9.7 divorces per 1,000 residents.
Other states with elevated divorce rates include Tennessee (8.4), Colorado (7.8), Wyoming (7.7), and Nebraska (7.6).
Southern Region Pattern: Higher divorce rates are widespread across the American South, with states like Alabama, Mississippi, and Arkansas consistently appearing near the top tier nationwide.

Alabama consistently ranks in the upper quartile of states nationwide for divorce rates.

Contributing Factors: Demographers note that Southern states, including Alabama, tend to have lower median ages at first marriage compared to the national average. Research links marrying at a younger age with greater marital instability over time, though age at marriage is just one of many underlying factors.

Over a multi-decade timeline, the proportion of married adults in the United States has experienced a noticeable decline:

Long-Term Shift: Today, roughly 46% to 51% of U.S. adults are married, down from nearly two-thirds in 1950.
Past Decade Trends: Over the past 10–15 years, annual marriage rates per 1,000 residents have largely stabilized, following a temporary dip caused by wedding postponements during the COVID-19 pandemic and a subsequent rebound.
Key Drivers: The broader decrease in the overall married population is primarily driven by:
Adults postponing first marriages until older ages.
Increased rates of cohabitation prior to or instead of legal marriage.
A growing percentage of never-married adults.

Despite changing national statistics on marriage timing, wedding traditions continue to adapt, with destination weddings growing in popularity. Beach settings—such as Alabama's scenic Gulf Shores and Orange Beach, alongside coastal hot spots across the Sunbelt—remain among the most sought-after wedding locations.

Picturesque Scenery: Waterfront backdrops provide natural aesthetics for photography and ceremonies without requiring elaborate venue decorations.
All-in-One Experience: Beach weddings allow couples to combine their ceremony, reception, and honeymoon into a single trip for guests and family.
Relaxed Vibe: Outdoor coastal ceremonies offer a more personal, intimate, and informal atmosphere compared to traditional ballroom settings.

While states like Utah lead the nation in high marriage rates, Oklahoma and several Southern states—including Alabama—record higher rates of divorce per capita. Though Americans are taking longer to walk down the aisle than previous generations, iconic settings like beach destinations remain a favorite venue for couples celebrating their special day.

text:
🌴 THE VICE FILES | EPISODE 6 | PART 3 😎

THE FINAL CONFRONTATION

DeMarco agrees to wear a concealed recording device during a meeting with Albert Lombard aboard his yacht.

The Vice squad hopes to obtain the evidence needed to bring down the mob boss.

But the operation begins unraveling.

The yacht leaves the dock, forcing the detectives to respond.

Under pressure, DeMarco reveals that he is wearing a wire.

The investigation is compromised.

Then an unexpected figure appears.

Jerry Carrow.

Still devastated by Barbara’s murder, Jerry has secretly boarded the yacht carrying a gun.

He has come looking for revenge.

Crockett realizes what is happening and attempts to intervene.

But Jerry shoots DeMarco dead.

The racketeer who framed Crockett is killed, destroying the detectives’ opportunity to secure the evidence they need against Lombard.

Although Lombard is briefly placed under arrest, the case against him has collapsed.

He expects to be released.

Jerry, meanwhile, faces the consequences of killing DeMarco.

Crockett and Tubbs have cleared Sonny’s name, but Barbara is dead, Jerry’s future is uncertain, and Lombard remains beyond their reach.

THE FINAL MOMENTS

Later, Crockett and Tubbs return to the St. Vitus Dance for some quiet fishing.

After everything they’ve experienced, the moment offers a brief escape from Miami’s criminal underworld.

No celebration.

No dramatic victory.

Just two detectives reflecting on a case where justice, revenge, and the law became painfully entangled.

THE VICE FILES | FINAL THOUGHTS

“One Eyed Jack” marks a defining moment in Miami Vice history.

Edward James Olmos makes his unforgettable debut as Lieutenant Martin Castillo.

His quiet intensity, discipline, and commanding presence immediately change the dynamic of the Vice squad.

Dennis Farina is equally memorable as Albert Lombard, a calculating mob boss whose influence allows him to escape meaningful consequences.

Joe Dallesandro portrays DeMarco as a ruthless racketeer whose arrogance ultimately contributes to his downfall.

Dan Hedaya adds tension as Internal Affairs investigator Ben Schroeder.

And Don Johnson and Philip Michael Thomas demonstrate why Crockett and Tubbs work so well together.

Sonny’s loyalty places him in danger, while Rico’s intelligence and undercover instincts help expose the deception.

But the episode’s greatest strength is its moral complexity.

Barbara is murdered.

Jerry seeks revenge.

DeMarco is killed.

Lombard escapes.

And Crockett, although cleared of corruption, is left with a victory that feels hollow.

Justice doesn’t always arrive the way we expect.

With Castillo now commanding the Vice squad, Miami Vice has entered a new era.

THE VICE FILES | EPISODE 6 COMPLETE

What did you think of “One Eyed Jack,” pal? Was Martin Castillo’s introduction the defining moment, or did Dennis Farina’s Albert Lombard steal the show?

See you out there, pal! 👇

text:
"Shipping costs near record highs are crushing Asian refining margins even as global fuel markets run short of supply. To keep Asian refiners buying, Middle Eastern exporters may have to absorb more of those costs themselves, squeezing the revenue they desperately need after months of war.
In yet another sign of the extraordinary distortions rippling through global ​energy markets as the US and Iran vie for control of the Strait of Hormuz, oil is increasingly flowing out of the Middle East, but actually getting it to customers has become so expensive ‌that it threatens to undermine the recovery.

The energy crisis has shifted decidedly from a shortage of crude to a shortage of refined fuels. Global refining throughput is set to fall by 2.3 million barrels per day this year to 81.7 million bpd, according to the International Energy Agency.
Many refineries have been damaged during the Middle East conflict, already in its eighth month, and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have compounded the squeeze. Diesel has felt the impact most acutely, with prices hitting all-time highs last month.
Asia has borne much of the pain from the ​Hormuz disruption. The region has historically relied on the Middle East for around 60% of its oil supplies. After the war began, many Asian refiners were forced to reduce operating rates and scramble for alternative crude ​from as far away as the United States and South America, at enormous cost.
Refiners elsewhere, particularly in the US and Europe, reaped the benefit as they ran at record ⁠levels while profit margins soared to record highs last month.
In theory, the recovery in Middle East oil exports in recent weeks should offer Asian refiners some much-needed relief. In practice, shipping economics are making that almost impossible.

FALSE DAWN
Crude shipments ​from the Middle East have risen significantly over the past six weeks. Total Middle Eastern crude exports, including volumes shipped through routes bypassing Hormuz, rose to 15.4 million bpd in September, nearly 90% of pre-war levels, according to Kpler data.
Much of ​that recovery came from transit through the strait itself. Flows through Hormuz climbed to 10.7 million bpd in September, around three-quarters of pre-war levels, as Gulf producers stepped up tanker transits under US Navy supervision.
Asian crude imports are also recovering and are set to reach 23.5 million bpd in October, their highest level since February and slightly above the 2025 average. Middle Eastern barrels account for about 10 million bpd of that total, according to Kpler.
Yet the rebound in crude supplies has not translated into healthier profits for Asian refiners. In ​some cases, margins are hovering close to zero, according to traders.
The devil is in the delivery.
Crude feedstock typically accounts for around 80% of a refinery's operating costs, while freight and insurance usually account for only around 3% to 7% ​of the delivered price of a barrel.
Not anymore.
Repeated Iranian attacks on tankers transiting Hormuz have sent freight rates and insurance premiums soaring. The attacks have also forced traders and producers to construct elaborate logistical workarounds, using fleets of tankers to shuttle crude out of ‌the Gulf ⁠and transfer cargoes between vessels.
This complex shuttle system requires so many tankers that it is limiting the vessels available globally and, in turn, driving freight rates sky-high well beyond the Middle East.

Asia is particularly vulnerable. Not only does the region depend heavily on Middle Eastern oil, but replacing those barrels with crude from the Atlantic Basin involves much longer voyages – and thus much higher costs.
Transporting a 2-million-barrel cargo from Nigeria to Singapore, for example, now costs around $32 a barrel, roughly eight times its pre-war level, according to LSEG data.
